subtopic: AGREEMENT FOR RECIPROCAL TRANSFER OF PENSION CREDITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join with Hon. James Allan, provincial treasurer of Ontario, in announcing a reciprocal agreement for the transfer of pension credits for civil servants transferring from the government of Canada to the province of Ontario or vice-versa.
This agreement is designed to assist a person wishing to transfer his employment from one government to the other to transfer at the same time the pension credits which are acceptable to the other government's pension plan. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs would the Prime Minister be in a position to advise whether the initiative taken by the Prime Minister of India, Mrs. Indira Gandhi, calling on Russia and Great Britain to reconvene immediately the 1954 Geneva conference on Indo China had been discussed with Canada before being announced by the Prime Minister of India? Also, is the Prime Minister aware of the fact that in the British house the foreign secretary mentioned this initiative, and that the British government would consider the Indian plan with sympathy and hope?

Does Canada support the basis upon which the Prime Minister of India asks for the reconvening of the conference, which is that all foreign troops must be withdrawn from Viet Nam; that Viet Nam must be insulated from what she calls "foreign interference", and that the Geneva conference should guarantee the integrity and independence of a neutral Viet Nam as well as of the neighbouring states of Laos and Cambodia?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition asked me yesterday whether I had received a resolution passed by the branch presidents of the Customs and Excise Officers' Association, and asked what was my reaction to this resolution. I did receive, on Monday last, a telegram listing a number of resolutions passed at the branch presidents' meeting last week end, and I have reviewed the contents of the telegram.
As I mentioned yesterday, the results of the pay revision announced last week will have the effect of removing a substantial number of employees from holding classifications, established as a result of the pay conversion program. Furthermore, the chairman of the staff side conference of the public service has endorsed and supports the pay revisions announced last week.
With respect to the second question asked by the right hon. gentleman regarding the government's position toward establishing a regulatory group distinct and separate from the clerical group, the government feels that the pay revision program should be completed as planned, and consideration for changes

Inquiries of the Ministry in the occupational groups should be postponed until the legislation concerning collective bargaining has been passed and initial experience demonstrates that changes are required.
All the questions raised in the telegram have been and will continue to be the subject of consultation between the independent Civil Service Commission, which is responsible for reclassification, the Treasury Board, which is responsible for final decisions on rates of pay, and the major employee organizations. These organizations include the staff side conference and the Civil Service Federation of Canada, to both of which the Customs and Excise Officers' Association is affiliated. Many of the problems involved are extremely complicated and will be worked out only as a result of hard work by all concerned in the normal process of consultation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CUSTOMS OFFICERS-PROTESTS RESPECTING CLASSIFICATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the minister answer the suggestion made in this telegram that as a result of the reclassification in the administrative sections to which reference is made by the president of the Customs and Excise Officers' Association, 40 per cent of their staff will find themselves reduced in so far as their salaries and allowances are concerned?

subtopic: CUSTOMS OFFICERS-PROTESTS RESPECTING CLASSIFICATION PROGRAM

Mr. Speaker, reclassification does not reduce the salary of any civil servant. What happens in the reclassification which is carried out by the independent Civil Service Commission, and which will increase the federal government payroll with regard to civil servants by 2 per cent, is that when persons are in a classification where they are red circled they will not receive advances until the classification has a ceiling beyond the salary they presently are receiving. In each case employees involved have the right of appeal to the Civil Service Commission with regard to classification.
I should like to point out also that many civil servants are being green circled rather than red circled, and their salaries are being increased.

subtopic: CUSTOMS OFFICERS-PROTESTS RESPECTING CLASSIFICATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Whether they are green circled, red circled or purple circled, is it a fact, as they allege, that 40 per cent will find themselves in a lesser position than today, and that the appeal of those who are dissatisfied will be to the very body that has fixed the order against which they complain?

The standing order which governs the time allocated to this debate is standing order 61A which reads as follows:
When a resolution preceding a bill involving the expenditure of public money has been referred to the committee of the whole house, the time allowed for consideration thereof in such committee shall not exceed one sitting day. For the purposes of this standing order, such a resolution shall be deemed to have been considered for one sitting day, provided the order to go into committee of the whole house is called as the first item under government orders on a Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, and provided it is continued, if necessary, until the normal time of adjournment on any such day. Such an order having been called on any Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, it shall have precedence over all other business until the time of adjournment on that day, unless it is disposed to earlier. Under any other circumstances, a total of five hours shall be deemed to be the equivalent of one sitting day.
This is the standing order by which the Chair is governed. If, however, it is the wish of the committee to do otherwise, I shall of course carry out the necessary procedure. Up to this point the Chair has not been advised of any agreement having been reached, other than what has been said in the committee this afternoon.

I was even more startled by the remarks yesterday of the hon. member for Kamloops, who gave us a very interesting and learned discourse on banking and financial policy. He did so in the never, never land of constitutional unreality, because he called for a number of reforms and courses of action without reference to the British North America Act.

For example, the hon. member did what the royal commission did and called for far greater control over what has become known as near-banks. I take it that the hon. member for Kamloops, in referring to near-banks, was referring to deposit-taking institutions. I should like to inform him, Mr. Chairman, that there are in the country only eight federally incorporated trust companies which are doing approximately one-third of the trust business in Canada. The huge trust companies such as National, Montreal, Royal, Crown and Trust General are all provincial institutions. I hope the hon. member for Kamloops is not suggesting that at the moment we in this house have the constitutional power to deal with those trust companies or near-banks.
We also have federally incorporated mortgage loan companies under the Companies Act. There are, I think, some 12 of those, some of which are deposit-taking institutions. They are doing two-thirds of the business, leaving about one-third for provincial institutions. I say, with regret, that we in this house do not have the power to pass amendments to the Bank Act to deal with these provincial institutions.
I am one of those, and I am sure the hon. member for Kamloops is, who favour more uniformity in our financial legislation and greater regulatory powers to deal with the various banks, near-banks, finance companies and loan companies. However, I say it is unrealistic for the hon. member for Kamloops and other hon. members opposite to make suggestions without reference to the constitution. I would remind them that we are discussing the revision of the Bank Act, not the revision of the British North America Act. Much as that act, in my view, needs amending and revising, much as the constitution needs revising, we are dealing with the Bank Act and not the constitution.

Bank Act
suggest it is too early to do something about the matter right now. That committee has carried on an exhaustive examination into the situation, and I think its report should be awaited by this house and by the Minister of Finance.
However, Mr. Chairman, I welcome the minister's statement that there will be a federal-provincial conference on the question of consumer credit. The question of interest disclosure, or truth in lending as it is often called, has become one which raises very difficult federal-provincial considerations. The recent decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, which I think put a very restrictive meaning on the word "interest", has further complicated the situation when dealing with actual consumer costs. Interest, in its restrictive sense, is only one small part of the total consumer credit cost and unless we in this house have the power to deal with interest and finance charges as a cost to consumers, we will be in difficulty.
We have seen other provinces taking action in the consumer credit field. I refer to Ontario, Alberta and New Brunswick. We in this house and the federal government itself have some constitutional authority in this regard. I would hope that we have a great deal, but the extent of our power is somewhat in question at the moment. Therefore, if we are to have a total approach to the protection of consumers against those who want to charge exorbitant and excessive consumer finance charges, we will need an integrated and co-ordinated federal-provincial approach which can only be arrived at under the aegis of a federal-provincial conference.
In referring to the revisions of the Bank Act I should like to make reference in the short time allowed me to only two other points. One is the right of banks to enter the conventional mortgage field and to take as security mortgages on real property.
We have heard from members opposite contentions that the revisions of the Bank Act must protect the little man or be concerned with the little man, and we have been criticized because our revisions do not do this. I suggest that one aspect of the revisions does take into account very seriously the situation of a great many small home owners in the country. During the period 1954-59 the chartered banks of Canada acquired a great many National Housing Act mortgages. The banks invested a great deal of their funds in this type of security. As the interest rate on National Housing Act mortgages went up, the banks withdrew from this field and at the

present time are virtually not lending any money for this type of mortgage because the interest rate on such mortgages exceeds the 6 per cent ceiling.
Under these revisions, Mr. Chairman, the banks will be allowed, as I think they should be, to take up this type of mortgage business again. A great problem is being faced by the many small home owners in this country who presently have their houses financed through National Housing Act mortgages. When they come to sell these houses they sell them on terms of cash to mortgage. As these mortgages are reduced or become amortized, it becomes increasingly difficult to get terms of cash to mortgage unless the homes are refinanced with another mortgage, which is not available from the banks today. Allowing the banks into this area will mean that home owners who are anxious to sell their houses and can only do so by refinancing will be able to refinance them through the present holder of the mortgage, namely, one of the chartered banks. By allowing the banks into this area, Mr. Chairman, we are also bringing about competition with the conventional mortgage lenders.
However, there is another important aspect which has not been mentioned in this debate. The chartered banks, by having thousands of branches across Canada located in every community, will be able to provide to people in those smaller communities mortgage services which are not available to them at the present time. Most of the big conventional mortgage lenders' offices are located in the large centres of Canada only and people living, for example, in Kamloops, Prince George, Nanaimo or Nelson in my own province have difficulty raising mortgage funds from conventional lenders. If the banks which are located in all these smaller centres are allowed into this area, this will provide the people there with a very much needed mortgage service.
Much has been said about the intimation of the minister that the bank interest ceiling rate will be raised. I suggest that this will increase the degree of competition existing between the banks and subsidiary lending institutions such as finance companies and loan companies.
I suggest that over the years, in building up what is undoubtedly one of the safest and most secure banking systems in the world, we have in fact placed our banks in a strait-jacket within which they must operate. I suggest that because the banks are in this strait-jacket, which we have imposed upon
July 7. 1966

them through legislation, the banking system of Canada is no longer serving the nation as it should. Because of this strait-jacket, we have seen over the years a fantastic and tremendous growth in near-banks, trust and loan companies and finance and acceptance corporations. At the same time, many of these corporations are filling needs which the banks must be allowed to fill if they are to serve the nation. Because of the strait-jacket into which we have put the banks, over the years they have become no longer able to fill the need for credit which exists. I suggest that we must remove or untie some of that strait-jacket and I contend that this is what the revisions will do.
Much has also been said by members on the opposite side of the house about the small businessman, the small farmer, the fisherman and the truck logger. I come from a province of such people, people who under the present Bank Act are unable by and large to go to a bank now and obtain credit or loans for their business operations in order to buy their trucks, farm equipment or fishing boats. Because of the restrictions imposed on the banks by the Bank Act, these people are forced into the hands of the loan sharks and acceptance companies, which are lending money obtained from banks at a low rate of interest to these farmers, small businessmen, truck loggers and fishermen at greatly increased and inflated interest rates. I suggest that by lifting the interest ceiling on the banks and allowing them to compete more effectively with the existing lending institutions, we will help these small people.

Mr. Chairman, one of the important objectives of the Conservative party is to do whatever we can to help bring down the interest rates which are paid by the average Canadian on the money he needs to operate his business or his farm, or for his own personal needs. We believe that this can be best done by bringing all lending institutions in Canada under the Bank Act, thus enabling them to operate under the same ground rules and to engage in all-out competition for the loan business of the Canadian people. We are convinced that this kind of competition will provide the lowest interest rates and the best service possible to the people of this country.
Bank Act
All financial institutions can be brought under the Bank Act by consultation with and co-operation by the provinces. It is just a question of sitting down and explaining what we have in mind and what objectives and benefits are to be derived therefrom. The provinces are just as anxious as we are to have the lending institutions under their jurisdiction come under the provisions of the Bank Act, because they know that this will make possible a general lowering of interest rates charged on loans to the people they represent in their provincial jurisdictions.
We all know that the interest rates which are charged on loans vary according to the security which the borrower is able to put up to secure his loan. Because of the differences existing in the various kinds of security that borrowers can provide, naturally there is a wide variation today in interest rates charged in all parts of the country. In merchandising goods and services, practice has clearly proved that prices are lower and service to the customer is better where competition for the customer's dollar is the keenest.
The same principle applies, of course, to the business of lending money. It was for that reason that the Porter Commission recommended that the best way to ensure the greatest availability of loans to the public and the lowest rates of interest on all types of loans would be for all lending institutions in Canada to be brought under the Bank Act. In this way, when this is done, they will be in a position to compete freely and fairly for the business of those who wish to borrow money in this country. Having talked to officials of a number of our chartered banks I know, as I am sure other hon. members know, that the banks would welcome this kind of competition against the near-banks for the loan dollar of the Canadian people.
In fields where greater competition between the banks and the near-banks has been allowed for instance, in the personal loan field, rates have been reduced very materially from somewhere around 18 per cent to approximately 10 per cent, which is a very important reduction indeed. If this kind of competition were allowed to take place for all types of loans the interest rate on the great majority of loans would be greatly reduced by the far greater competition which there would be for this business.
We in the Conservative party agree with the recommendations of the Porter Commission which was established by our government some years ago to develop thinking and

July 7. 1966
Bank Act
recommendations for such time as the Bank Act would come under revision. We strongly condemn the present government for not carrying out the recommendations of that commission, recommendations which were clearly and carefully thought out after many months of extremely hard and careful work. We condemn the government for not incorporating the commission's recommendations in the legislation now before the house.
Turning to the resolution we are debating today we see that it provides for a raising of the bank rate according to a formula which is not based on any business principle geared to the needs of business or agriculture. We are reliably informed that the formula was worked out a very short time ago after a great deal of controversy within the government and is geared far more to bringing harmony to the warring factions within the government party than to any business or economic need. This resolution completely disregards the most important recommendation contained in the report of the Porter Commission, which was that the removal of the interest rate ceiling must be coupled with bringing the near-banks under the Bank Act.
Today, Mr. Chairman, as we in this house know very well, industry and agriculture in all parts of the country are suffering from the tight money policy which has been imposed by this government. This policy is making it impossible for many farmers and businessmen to obtain the capital they need to carry out the normal business expansion they must carry out each year in order to handle the additional business which a growing economy in a country such as Canada makes available to them. If they are not able to expand and take advantage of the additional sales which they could otherwise make, these sales, particularly in the export market, will go to other customers in other countries and they will be very difficult, if not impossible, to regain.
Anyone who has been in business knows that once a customer becomes used to dealing with somebody else, he will very likely find out that the other person can provide just as good a standard of service, or perhaps better, than you can, and the customer tends to remain with the other supplier even though you are able to come back into the market and offer him your goods again. The only way that our farmers and industrialists can cut costs and thereby make a better return on the capital and labour they put into their operations is to expand production and, by
[Mr. Hees.J
making use of the economies of scale, cut their initial costs as much as possible.
We in the Conservative party are convinced that the proper role for government to play in business and agriculture today is to help these people about whom I have spoken help themselves in every way possible. We believe that the government should be assisting our businessmen and our farmers in every way possible to expand their operations, thereby providing more jobs for our people and more prosperity for our country.
We believe that the best way to do this is to take steps to provide adequate credit at the lowest possible rates of interest. This, we are convinced, will be done if all our financial institutions are brought under the Bank Act, as was strongly urged by the report of the Porter Commission. If this is done these financial institutions will be able to enter into fair and wide open competition for the lending dollar of the Canadian people. This, we are convinced, will result in the average Canadian being able to borrow the money he needs at a considerably lower rate of interest than he has to pay today.
We in this party have decided that when this government does decide to follow the recommendations of the commission that was set up to give very deep and penetrating study to this matter and when it decides to bring the near-banks under the Bank Act and thereby make possible a general lowering of interest rates by greater competition, we shall then be very pleased indeed to support this measure. Until then we intend to oppose it.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is always strange to hear a minister being criticized for doing what the critics are accusing him of not doing. If there is any criticism to be made of the minister it is that he has slavishly followed the Porter Commission recommendations. If we examine the proposals he has introduced we will find they have been taken almost word for word from the report of that commission. The argument about whether or not near-banks should be brought under federal jurisdiction is, I suspect, a piece of camouflage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite should save their applause; I have some things to say about which they may feel differently. The advisability of bringing nearbanks under federal jurisdiction is questionable at this time though one might well be tempted to ask the government why it does not try to do so. The government has indicated its intention to introduce this legislation and there will be time in the months ahead to consider carefully what precisely is meant by "bank" and what authority the federal government possesses in this field. These questions might well be referred to a court which could adjudicate upon them, because I think definitions of this kind are badly needed.
With the exception of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, who hinted at it, everybody seems to have overlooked the fact that the federal government does have clear-cut jurisdiction over interest rates under the British North America Act. If the federal government were really serious about regulating the financial institutions of this country it would have no need for any jurisdiction or authority beyond that which it already possesses.
I suggest to the minister that the federal government could, if it wished, control interest rates throughout Canada and that it is within the framework of its authority to do so. If the minister does not do so in this particular case, it is a clear indication that he has no intention of using control over interest rates in order to remedy national problems as he sees them.
Bank Act
We should be well advised to take a careful look at the sugar-coated pill which the doctor is introducing into this house and intends to administer to the Canadian people. He has made some accommodations. He has suggested certain reforms which are long overdue, and in these areas some credit is due him. I have in mind particularly the hidden reserves of banks. For the first time in Canada we have a Minister of Finance who is beginning to realize that this business of hidden reserves has not always worked to the benefit of the Canadian people and of the tax collectors of this country. I am pleased an attempt will now be made to obtain disclosure of information concerning the relationship between profits and hidden reserves.
The sugar coating covering this measure does, however, hide an extremely bitter centre. At the core of this entire measure is the question of interest rates. Whatever may be said about the fringes, at the heart of this legislation is the question: what will happen to interest rates? Will they rise, will they fall, or will they be allowed to float with the market?
What is happening here is typical of what is happening to the Liberal party. By permitting this legislation to come forward as an instrument of their policy the Liberal party is moving unequivocally to the right. Any idea that there might be a left wing or reform movement within that party should now be completely dispelled. I do not hold the minister responsible for this. The Minister is a right-winger; he has an integrity of his own, and what he has brought in is a right-wing policy.
I listened with some sadness the other evening to the hon. member for St. John's West when he talked about the needs of his particular area, criticized some members of this house for wishing to return to a laissez-faire economy and welcomed the fact that the government was prepared to play a role in Canadian finance. Mr. Speaker, this is exactly what is not happening. Perhaps the hon. member for St. John's West should have a heart to heart talk with the Minister of Finance. What his minister has in effect said is that we are now returning completely to a laissez-faire economy. The controls which now exist will be dropped in favour of market regulation and the only restraints, the only restrictions, will be what the traffic can bear and what the market will accommodate itself to accepting.

July 7, 1966
Bank, Act
Our economy has its problems and it is interesting to see the way in which the minister, after an analysis of those problems, has arrived at solutions. Questions have been asked in the house many times concerning the shortage of mortgage money in Canada. We know there is such a shortage. We know the cost of mortgage money has risen. The minister's answer to these questions-and he has only one answer-is: First, we shall raise the ceiling, then we shall free the rate and the competition will take care of the situation.
I suggest to the minister that this is not what will happen. In some circumstances such as a major recession-and I suspect the minister knows the circumstances-the applying of these rates in an economy where some elements are competing fiercely for money might lead to those levels finding a proper and just point at which to settle. But we are moving toward a managed economy to a considerable extent, an economy within which no government will permit a serious recession to take place. It is obvious that interest rates cannot be completely fluid in circumstances of this kind.
We know the banks are lent out. All financial institutions are lent out. How will the minister get more mortgage money unless it is diverted from other sources? How will he get cheaper money in the circumstances he is developing for us? If the bank rate in this situation is freed from restriction or permitted to increase, I have no hesitation in saying that Canada will face the highest interest rates, the highest cost of money, in all history.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Nobody can say where that level will settle, whether it will be 1 per cent more, 2 per cent more, or what. If in this situation the bank rate goes up by 1 per cent you may rest assured that the trust companies, the nearbanks and other financial institutions will increase their rates by that differential and in effect what you will have is a competition for money.

Mr. Minister, you too are a very distinguished member of this house despite the fact that you are a right-winger. Being a right-winger does not make you any more or less distinguished. It is merely an indication of the way you think.
Returning to the question of mortgage money I would refer to an article in the Financial Post of July 22 headed "Mortgage Drought Is A Red-Hot Issue Now," which quoted a Toronto businessman as saying:
I won't pay 71 per cent-8 per cent for a mortgage. If I can't do better, I'll have to forget about buying a house for the time being.
I assume that Toronto businessman is doing a little better than the fellow who works in a factory; yet he cannot afford to buy a house now. So what happens to the fellow working in a factory if interest rates go up, and they will go up under the conditions described by the minister?
If interest rates on mortgages increase from 7 per cent to 8 per cent this means a difference of $106 per year. In other words a 1 per cent rise costs the home owner $106 per year. Translated into weeks this comes to $2 extra per week. But if the working man goes out and says he needs more money, then everybody in the country suddenly throws up their hands at the spectacle of the dreadful working man asking for more money.
From the viewpoint of inflation, how much more inflationary can anything be? Take that extra cost in every business and pass it on to the consumer and you really have got a cost-wage spiral position, and there will be nobody to blame but the minister for introducing this kind of legislation. I hope the minister will remember this if he hears the cry that the working man needs more money and is asking for more money. In that case I
July 7, 1966

Bank Act
hope the minister will be very sympathetic to the working man's demands. He should be, because if this legislation goes through in its present form he will be largely responsible for the inflation that will take place.
The minister says that the necessity of removing the ceiling on the rate is so that small businessmen will be not be the victims of loan sharks. This is very commendable and I appreciate the minister's concern for small businessmen. Everyone in this chamber shares the same concern. But is the minister really helping the small businessman? Has he discovered the percentage of small businessmen who are really going to the sharks and paying high interest? If the minister would take a statistical look he would find that the vast majority of small businessmen still go to the banks and get accommodation from them. If the bank rate is raised the vast majority of small businessmen will be hurt, and the increased cost they will pay for money will be passed on to the public.
If the minister wants to correct the abuses that exist in the system, and there are abuses, I again mention the remedy I suggested which is within the minister's jurisdiction, namely, control interest rates in Canada. The federal government has the authority to control them. We can do it in the same way as we do under the Small Loans Act and the Moneylenders Act. If the minister is going to have a managed economy from the fiscal point of view he should also consider it from a monetary point of view, and I suggest this is a more useful instrument for ensuring that Canada would not become an expensive money country, certainly more useful than freeing the rate and letting the market determine what interest rates should be.
We have also heard that the bank rate has to be freed in order to help consumers who borrow money. On this point I might digress for a minute to say that one of the most salutary events that has taken place has been the entry of the banks into the consumer lending field. They have done an admirable, excellent job despite the fixed 6 per cent interest rate. As we all know, that rate is not maintained in this field. The banks cannot engage in that kind of business at 6 per cent, but their entry into this field has been most useful. It should be encouraged. But why do we have to take the interest ceiling off in a blanket way? Why remove it completely?
Why couldn't the banks be freed of the ceiling in the area of consumer lending and allowed a special rate? Even in the area of
mortgage lending they could have a special rate. There is no reason to believe that the banks have to be either restricted or completely free. There are intermediate ways of accomplishing the necessary objectives.
However, the minister has taken a look at a situation that needs correcting and has come up with a one-note answer-free the interest rate. This is supposed to be a new panacea, but it is only a return to 18th century mercantilism. That is not good enough. If the minister is doing this with the thought in the back of his mind that by making Canada a high interest rate country he can attract foreign capital, then he had better tell us so.
Because my time allotment has almost expired I want to reserve the last few minutes for a brief summation of what I think the effects of the Bank Act revision will be. To remove the interest ceiling without proper safeguards is to raise the cost of every single thing in this country. It is to put the cost of money in Canada at a height it has never achieved previously, and one that no one at this point can calculate. Interest rates of 8 per cent and 9 per cent on commercial lending may be possible through this type of approach. The present 6 per cent ceiling on the banks may be rigid, may in some ways be unfair and may require some changes, but to remove the only protection we have and not bring in some other assurance that there will be regulatory factors in the economy, is to invite a disaster of the greatest proportion for everyone who uses and needs money in Canada.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
If the minister feels that some rates have to be increased then the minister alone should not determine what that increase shall be. He should set up a board to which those who require the increase, and who can present a good argument for it, can come, and it can then be decided in the national interest whether such an interest rate should be permitted. One way or another an increase in the interest rate will affect the entire cost of living in this country. Everyone, whatever he may do and whatever he may buy, will be affected because interest rates are as much a component in the cost of products as is labour. If he is concerned about low-cost housing he might as well forget about it. It will be dead. There will be no low-cost housing and there will be no medium-priced housing. There will only be high-cost housing in this country.

Mr. Chairman, it was important to introduce before the recess the resolution dealing with the decennial revision of the Bank Act and the extension of the existing charters until July 1, 1976.
After first reading, all those who are interested will have the opportunity to study the bill. And, as stated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), they will be able, later this fall, to express their views and recommendations to the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs to which it will be referred.
This bill affects practically all Canadians, because banking operations play a vital part in our economic and social life and our banks must be able to play that part without being hindered by obsolete legislation which does not take into account today's economic realities.
Our banking system is fortunately, as mem tioned by several hon. members, one of the best in the world, but it is certainly possible to improve it to the greater benefit of the people in general. It is readily agreed that our banks play a very important role. And

our hopes for greater economic independence in the future may depend on the way the government will legislate in the banking field. We are already late in making this revision, but in 1964 when the bank charters expired, it was necessary to extend them in order to be able to study the long and complex report which the royal commission on banking and finance had just submitted.
It is a very detailed and exhaustive study which constitutes an excellent work of reference and the fact that it is approximately seven times heavier than the MacMillan report published 30 years ago shows to what extent our financial system has become complicated.
Of course, that shows the commissioners' very commendable preoccupation to present a complete report. In 1965, the adjournment of both houses prevented the study in committee of the bill after the resolution stage. After what the Minister of Finance has said, it seems that the government has decided to limit and prevent foreign control of Canadian banks. And that decision will meet with the approval of all those who take an interest in our economic future, because previously nothing prevented a foreign bank from acquiring an important part of the shares, if not all of them, of an existing Canadian bank.
If, on the one hand, customers could derive some benefit from the fact that those banks might bring new ideas and initiatives, a different way of doing business, however, they would certainly be less receptive and sympathetic when it came to following the recommendations and suggestions of the Canadian authorities as pointed out in the report of the Porter commission.
Moreover, it would be disastrous for many Canadian businesses whose operations might be transferred elsewhere. If a bank, for instance, were controlled by American interests, it could then easily obtain the patronage of a Canadian subsidiary, of a company which would already be its customer in the United States.
The government wants to encourage the greatest competition and variety possible in the service of loans and savings to meet the needs of Canadians during the next decade. And this can be done by allowing an increase in the number of banks in Canada; the government has wisely decided that the new banks will have to be in the hands of Canadians.
July 7, 1966

It had been recommended by the royal commission on banking and finance, which is based on the experience of several generations of banking transactions, that the Bank Act be extended so as to include several institutions which are not subject to it now, and which are under the provincial jurisdiction instead.
It is certain, Mr. Chairman, that several of our institutions could come within the banking system without its soundness being affected, and they would benefit thereby, but the important question of the constitutionality of that measure must be taken into consideration and the government has taken a wise course in attempting to incite them to come freely within our banking system. This is certainly a field where there should be co-operation and consultation between the various levels of government.
The minister has given to understand that the provinces or their agencies will henceforth be allowed to invest in bank shares without voting privileges and I think he is well advised to open such an investment opportunity to provincial funds, because normally a province or one of its agencies should be empowered to invest all their funds in gilt-edged bank stocks and there is no reason to deprive them of this right in the present circumstances.
The minister has also announced a federal-provincial conference on consumer credit this fall and I hope that, by then, it may be possible to come to an agreement to require all credit firms throughout the country to indicate and clearly publish the actual interest charges, so that all credit institutions, whether under federal or provincial control, may be on the same footing and obliged to disclose the actual rates charged to the customer for any given period.
The Minister of Finance is providing for changes in the reserves which the chartered banks are required to maintain with the Bank of Canada and it is his intention to reduce these. Such reserves, made up of an 8 per cent statutory reserve and a secondary reserve equivalent to 15 per cent of all deposits payable in Canadian funds held by the chartered banks, leave them in an unfavourable position as regards the competition of other banking institutions not subject to such restrictions, and the royal commission has recommended a lowering of the cash ratio. Considering that the protection of the depositing public is involved, I hardly think

there can be any question of eliminating
them.
It was also announced that the government intends to prevent the directors of a bank from sitting on the board of another bank, and also to prohibit all agreements between banks on the interest to be charged on loans or to be paid on deposits and this measure should encourage free competition between such institutions so that the public may benefit from the best possible yield.
Because of the ceiling on interest rates and of other restrictions in the Bank Act preventing them, for instance, from granting mortgage loans, the banks closely associated themselves with trust, mortgage, loan, investment companies and others. It has been specified, I believe, that chartered banks will not be allowed to have more than a 10 per cent equity ownership in a Canadian corporation. It may be necessary to read the bill to obtain further details, but through the amendments to be made to the act, banks should not find it necessary to get involved so much with competitive financial institutions. In order to promote competition, it is necessary to control the purchase of shares, mergers or the establishment of subsidiary or satellite companies.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to discuss all proposed or commendable amendments, but rather deal briefly with the two main questions of greater concern to the average citizen and which seriously hinder free competition: first, the interdiction to grant mortgage loans, a provision to be deleted, and
then,	the ceiling on interest rates which is being changed and may be adjusted according to the economic situation of the country.
The fact that banks will be allowed in the future to grant mortgage loans at the current market rate is welcome news, because the present situation was unsatisfactory, both for the public and for the banks. The latter never had that power, except since 1954, with the exception of loans granted under the National Housing Act. They did not hesitate then to enter into that new field and loaned over one billion dollars, which proves that with their network of branches throughout the country, they can render tremendous services to the people in that connection.
However, when the rate of interest on such loans was set at more than 6 per cent, they had to withdraw from the market, due to the ceiling being imposed on them. The coming of banks into this important segment of our

July 7, 1966
Bank Act
economy will promote greater competition and activity and will contribute to check any increase in interest rates by making available new capital in the field of mortgage loans.
This will also allow them to improve their commercial loans services, particularly with regard to small businessmen who, thanks to this additional guarantee, will be able to borrow greater amounts and more easily from the banks, at a rate certainly more advantageous than elsewhere. Big mortgage companies undeniably grant loans more easily in large cities than in small municipalities and distant regions. Local institutions such as credit unions, which are familiar with the needs and characteristics of a given region, give very efficient service there, and the banks, thanks to their branches here and there, will also be able to help decentralize mortgage funds and balance investments in the various regions.
I also hope that, in the future, private institutions, like those of the government, for example the Industrial Development Bank, will expand and improve the services they give small enterprise by putting at their disposal economic and technical advisers and giving them financial information and advice, so as to help them manage and control their business better. This legislation concerning mortgage loans will be welcomed by all and will undoubtedly improve service in this respect.
Mr. Chairman, according to what the hon. Minister of Finance indicated, the 6 per cent ceiling on the bank rate will be periodically readjusted until conditions on the money market improve, when it can be eliminated.
In introducing the resolution in May 1965, the former minister of finance had specified that, if there were a general increase of the rate of interest in the future, the government would then review the situation. Since then rates have increased considerably, quarterly treasury loans, for example, increasing from 3.82 in 1965 to a recent 5.10, and rates of interest must now be considered in a totally different perspective.
Nobody can dispute, Mr. Chairman, that the existing rate of 6 per cent does not correspond to the current rate: indeed, it was set up during a period when the conditions of the capital market were very different from what they are today. It favours the use of indirect means and the multiplication of related financial institutions that escape that ceiling and

are not under the control of the federal authorities.
The current rate of 6 per cent applicable to commercial loans, that is loans to small businesses, small industries and small businessmen, works against those whom the law intends to protect against the abuses of lenders, and compels them to turn to companies charging higher and often excessive rates of interests. One needs only to be convinced to read the reports of the finance companies which, in recent years, have multiplied average-term commercial loans. The progressive and controlled increase of the ceiling would certainly have the effect of balancing the capital market and, by extending the field of action of banks, the competition will help to limit that of institutions with much less control and responsibility than our banks.
The fear of those who anticipate a general increase of interest rate as a result of this measure is not justified and is indeed denied by the great majority of experts. The future will show, I am sure, that that fear was not founded. Such an increase in the ceiling would rather adjust and balance the rates. Actually, that was the main recommendation of the Porter commission; page 364 and the following pages of the report set forth major and convincing arguments in favour of a higher ceiling, and I quote:
The 6 per cent interest rate ceiling introduces undesirable rigidity in the financial system and hampers and distorts the working of markets. It also has arbitrary effects on the institutions' competition for business and on their ability to serve the community well which were not contemplated when the ceiling was originally introduced and subsequently amended.
We recommend that it be removed regardless of other changes in the legislation. The ceiling stands in the way of flexible lending by the banks in that it frequently prevents them from making loans on which higher rates must be charged to cover administrative costs and risks. Obviously, this is to the banks' disadvantage; more importantly, however, it discriminates against borrowers such as small businesses which, if they are to obtain funds at all, must turn to the other lenders which charge rates well above those the banks would ask if free to do so.
Mr. Chairman, another group of independent experts, the Economic Council of Canada, supported unreservedly that attitude, and in its Second Annual Review, page 187, made the following statement:
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
More generally, to minimize distortions and instabilities in credit and financial markets, and to ensure easier access by homebuilders, consumers and small business to credit, various recommendations of the royal commission on banking and
July 7, 1966

Bank Act
finance deserve careful attention-including measures to promote more competitive credit conditions, and removal of the arbitrary 6 per cent interest rate ceiling which currently forces many small borrowers into loans at much higher rates.
The vast majority of financial and economic experts hold this opinion as well. It has also been claimed that banks already show large profits and that this measure will only serve to increase them even more. Now, the government can easily control them and reach them, through taxes on profits or otherwise; at any rate, it is not a logical reason for preventing them from playing a more efficient and more advantageous role with regard to the people generally, and the financial system of our country. This would be preferable to transferring those powers or leaving them to similar institutions at a higher cost to the public.
In order to enlarge their share of the market in the face of competition, banks will have to improve their services, make loans at reasonable rates and pay higher rates of interest on savings. In order to obtain additional funds, they will have to increase the rate of interest on deposits, thus benefitting millions of people who, as a precautionary measure and for security, entrust their money to banks. Incidentally, more open competition might be favourable to banks but, above all, the good of the community as a whole must be considered and promoted.
The Minister of Finance, who has already given us proof of his experience, his competence and wisdom, has once more formulated a realistic, practical and constitutional policy, to enable our banking institutions to make an even greater contribution to the progress and growth of our country; a policy that will also contribute to the economic and social well being of the Canadian people as a whole.
This act, Mr. Chairman, will bring progress to our financial system in its evolution, will give it greater flexibility, firmness, dynamism and competitive stamina; the Minister of Finance must certainly be congratulated.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest as the hon. member who spoke before me talked about the banking system, about the services rendered by banks to industry, business, individuals, etc. Strangely enough, there seems to be an attempt to compare banks to other Canadian financial institutions; to compare a bank to an ordinary finance company, when the two are absolutely not similar.
Ordinary finance companies must have in their tills the amounts they can lend or wish to lend, while chartered banks do not have to have in the till the huge amounts they lend.
Last night, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) spoke at great length on this resolution and on these amendments to the Bank Act. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has read the speech made by his parliamentary secretary, he must have died laughing this morning. His dear parliamentary secretary blundered, he contradicted himself flagrantly, he made about the most ridiculous speech ever delivered here in this house. Indeed he said;
This decennial revision will certainly be welcomed by the newspapers and the public as the most radical measure since the institution of the Bank of Canada about 30 years ago. It will likely increase the confidence of the public in our banking institutions and in any future decisions of the government concerning the monetary policy of our country.
And then he added:
It is easy to note that the Minister of Finance has decided to implement the necessary reforms for such a competition between all levels of financial institutions in Canada, and I think he should be very warmly commended.
A little further, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) stated:
The 6 per cent ceiling was adopted some forty years ago-
Well, 40 years ago the ceiling was at
5	per cent. A bank could not charge more than 5 per cent interest on a loan. Here he said:
Under the present system, Mr. Chairman, big borrowers definitely have an edge over small people who need money. As banks have become the cheapest source of capital supply for corporate and individual borrowers, since there is a 6 per cent ceiling on interest rates, there developed recently a practice which clearly discriminates against small borrowers.
And he went on to say:
Generally speaking, the small borrower who comes to a bank gets a loan at a rate higher than
6	per cent.
Please note that the small borrower who goes to a bank where the ceiling is 6 per cent manages to get funds at a rate higher than 6 per cent since the banks have found a legal way out. I wonder if the minister agrees with that. The banks have found a legal procedure which allows them to make personal loans at 9 and 10 per cent. It means that the small borrowers we are trying to protect by setting the rate at 6 per cent

July 7, 1966
Bank Act
are not protected at all by the present banking regulations. Such is the statement made by the secretary to the Minister of Finance last night: the ceiling is 6 per cent but legally the banks have succeeded in making loans at 9 and 10 per cent.
At the beginning of my remarks, I said that the banks are lending something they do not have. If a bank has a $100 million reserve with the Bank of Canada, it has the right under the federal legislation-and I am calling the Minister of Finance to witness what I am saying now-to lend $1.4 billion, based on the $100 million reserve with the Bank of Canada. And it has the right to ask for 6 per cent on $1.3 billion it has just created.
The bank has the power to do that. That means $78 million in interest for a year; $390 million for five years; and $1.56 billion for 20 years, whereas the bank had only $100 million in reserve with the Bank of Canada.
That is the power of the chartered banks in Canada. It cannot be compared at all with that of the other loan companies. And if the minister is so solicitous about the small Canadian borrowers, then instead of removing the ceiling on the interest rates charged by the banks, why does he not force the finance companies to reduce their usurious interest rates to protect the small borrower whom the government wants to protect, as it is trying to make us believe, with this bill.
Mr. Chairman, there is a way to help the small people, and it is certainly not by helping the big people to get bigger that you will help the small people. We live under a system where the big people get bigger in smaller numbers and where the small ones get smaller in greater numbers, and no solution is found to that problem. Let us reduce the interest rate and force the finance companies to reduce their interest rates instead of allowing them to charge 24, 20 or 15 per cent interest, and let us impose a ceiling on those companies.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Another thing could help the small borrowers: why does the Department of Finance or the federal government allow the banks to create a shortage of money and credit in Canada? Why? If the government assumed its responsibilities and told the banks: We need so much credit for the normal business of the country and you will create the credit or we will do it through the Bank of Canada. It would be a solution but the government does not do that. Instead, to help the small

people, it allows the banks to increase the interest rate.
Another way for the government to help the little fellow would have been to stop gathering the savings of the small and average citizens, and to leave them in circulation. Instead of piling them up here, in Ottawa, the government should help, for instance, in lowering income tax. No, the government does not think of that. It introduces a bill to amend the Act. This is the greatest monetary reform since the creation of the Bank of Canada. Imagine, in the twentieth century, in 1966, to tell us that in the House of Commons. Why? Because the majority of government members understand nothing of the mechanism of chartered banks of Canada.
I understand that one may laugh but it is believed that the chartered banks are financial institutions like the Traders Finance, the Household Finance, the Beneficial Finance and any other finance company. But it is not true. The finance companies, the "caisses populates" the savings banks, cannot lend more than what they have. However, the chartered banks can lend any amount even what they do not have. They can take my own savings and multiply them by 14 to lend to the public at 6 per cent. Six per cent interest on credit created out of nothing is not enough. That is what control by the chartered banks means in Canada.
I understand and I repeat it, the finance companies practice usury; I understand that. The government has the power to bring these people to book. Mr. Chairman, I realize that this bill in abolishing the ceiling on interest rates for chartered banks agrees to direct theft, legalized by the federal government. Instead of simply allowing the thief to remain as it is, it gives him the means to grow bigger. The small thief goes to jail. As for the big thief, the financier, let us allow him to charge more interest. That is the fine monetary reform of the federal government. It has been spelled out in full and explained by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance himself said the day before yesterday that the rate of interest is too low and should obviously be raised to help such borrowers, and that banks must be able to compete with private lenders.
Mr. Chairman, what is to prevent banks from lending to whomever they please? I do business with finance companies, with Traders Finance.
July 7, 1966

We are told here: When the rate of interest is higher, banks will lend more easily to small borrowers. The borrower who wants a loan at 6 per cent and who does not seem to have all the security required by the bank does not get a loan. If the rate of interest were 8 per cent, does the minister think this man would then be able to get a loan? No. I know of one particular case where a man went to a chartered bank to borrow a sum of money to pay for a car. The bank manager told him: My friend, you do not have enough security for a loan. Then this person went to the Household Finance Company, borrowed the money to pay for his car, signed a promissory note attached to his contract including interest, insurance, and so on. Household Finance took this note to a Canadian chartered bank, whether the Royal Bank of Canada, the Canadian National Bank or the Toronto-Dominion. The bank accepted the note of this same man who was not solvent ten minutes ago and bought it at a discount rate of 85 to 90 per cent. This means that the finance company immediately got all of its capital plus part of the interest charged. Immediately. This man who, according to the bank, was not solvent ten minutes ago-how is it that his credit is better at 24 per cent? Why does the bank accept his note from the finance company, but not directly from him? Mr. Chairman, we will be told again that an increased rate of interest would allow banks to help small borrowers more. That is not true. The banks do not help the small borrowers but the big ones, as the Minister of Finance is well aware.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance made another point the other day. The banks must reveal their hidden reserves. They do not pay taxes on them at the moment. How would the minister force the banks to declare their hidden funds? What means would the government use. They do not tell us. We are told: We will take the necessary measures; we will request the banks to declare their hidden funds on which they do not pay any taxes at present.
Mr. Chairman, the minister nods his head. But by what means will he accomplish this, since the banks have done many things behind this government's back, and behind the former government's back? The banks have always played hide and seek with the government. And today, the minister tells us: We will force the banks to declare their hidden funds. By what means will we do so? Everyone has to declare his income. Everyone is supposed to
Bank Act
declare hidden income; yet, a large number of Canadians hide money away. Not only banks, oh no. There are others still who do not declare anything to the government.
How is the government going to find out who hides money with a view to evading income tax? Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary to the minister added this, yesterday:
It follows that the 6 per cent bank loan market is available to two particular types of borrowers, that is small businessmen and industrialists.
What an amazing discovery.
As banks are limited to a 6 per cent ceiling, there is absolutely no leeway possible.
Poor banks. Up against a depression. Will higher rates improve slums in Canada? Let the minister compare bank buildings in in Canada with the dwellings of little old Canadians who have to borrow money. Then you can tell me if those poor banks are to be pitied so. I have nothing against banks that deal with the public on a private basis, that is all very well. Provincial or federal governments, or school boards, should not have to kotow before a chartered bank that has the power to create credit 14 times the amount it holds in reserve. But let the Bank of Canada service public undertakings; and let chartered banks continue to serve private enterprise, not at exhorbitant rates of interest, not at rates without a ceiling, but at a rate that has a ceiling. When that ceiling was 6 per cent, banks did not starve to death. They knew no economic recession, they did not suffer. But the Canadians suffered.
Mr. Chairman, I maintain the monetary reform advocated by the Minister of Finance is nothing but a hoax. And some people believe in it. A while ago, a member made a speech on banks, on those poor banks which do not have the right to ask the same rate of interest as the small private companies. There was applause because people do not know what control banks have in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, Social Credit has a solution, it may still provoke laughter, but he who laughs last laughs best, because, Mr. Chairman, in the present system, with unrequited strikes right and left, if one seeks the root of the problem, one will find a question of money and credit and so long as the present or future governments fail to alter the present financial system in order to make money serve mankind instead of forcing mankind to serve money, grave days, dangerous days are in the offing for Canada as other countries of the world have experienced.

July 7, 1966
Bank Act
If we must perforce follow in the footsteps of world revolutions, very well. But if we can avoid this, if we can react soon enough to bring about monetary and fiscal reform so that money and credit may serve the people then, Mr. Chairman, we will have saved the country and specially the Canadian people, which is what counts in the long run.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize the time left in the debate on this resolution is rather short so I will attempt to keep my remarks to a minimum in order to allow at least one other speaker to take part in the discussion.
The resolution before the committee provides for the decennial revision of the Bank Act, a revision which is already two years late, and will extend the charters of the present banks to July 1, 1976.
Apart from the remarks of the Minister of Finance, the details of the present legislation are not known. The minister has outlined his policies relating to the legislation which is to

follow this resolution. He has enunciated some points with which we agree and some others which we do not find acceptable. But we do say that this resolution should pass in order that the legislation can come before us.
At this point I would urge the Minister of Finance-I believe that if he will do this all members of the committee will be in agreement-to refer the subject matter of this resolution to the standing committee so that it can get down to the hard work which must be done in coming to the highest common denominator of agreement so far as the legislation is concerned. After that work has been completed the matter can come back to the house for final decision. If this is done I am sure that much of the committee work can be accomplished while the house is in recess.
However, the passage of this resolution does not mean, and I make this very clear, that we are in agreement in principle with what may be the policies of the minister in the legislation. We are in agreement with the principle that the Bank Act must be revised and that this legislation must be passed before the end of this session. We in our party believe that the subject matter of this resolution should go to the committee as quickly as possible. We should not wait until after second reading before making such referral because there would not be sufficient time then to debate the decisions that are made in the committee.
Perhaps the most important revelation was when the minister said that the banks will be required to disclose their inner reserves. To this we give our complete agreement. These hidden reserves represent a privilege which has been grossly abused. Therefore we believe that the minister is to be commended for this announcement. Likewise, it is good that the different banks will be prohibited from making agreements on interest rates on both loans and deposits.
We in the Social Credit party also agree that the interlocking of bank directorates should be prohibited. We believe also that the relaxing of restrictions prohibiting banks from participating in the area of mortgage loans is fair and sound. The minister outlined his policies, some of which we believe are good. However, there are others with which we cannot agree.
The reduced cash reserves allowing flexibility in reserve requirements can only be fair if the near-banks are likewise brought under the umbrella of this banking legislation. If the Minister of Finance really means
July 7, 1966

Bank Act
that greater competition is a good thing for banking, then it seems to us that he must also include those institutions, other than credit unions and treasury branches, operating in the same areas as the banks, and they should be brought within the legislation controlling banking with which we will be concerned when this resolution has passed.
The second major area of difference, and the one which is the most vital in my opinion, is the decision to lift the 6 per cent interest ceiling on bank loans. With this we cannot agree. The banks have advanced a strong argument in favour of this policy. They have developed the argument that by lifting the ceiling on bank loans there would be a general reduction in interest rates. True, it would lower the interest rates presently charged on mortgages through trust and finance companies, which today are operating at rates of 8 to 12 per cent and in some areas even as high as 20 per cent and more. These interest rates are wrong. They are immoral and unjust. Yet we must seek to correct the problem at the top level and not just equalize the situation by raising the bottom level.
I believe that the desired objective of lower bank interest rates rather than raising them can be better effected by including those institutions which to day are operating at extremely high interest rates under banking legislation, so that the total picture of interest rates will be reduced. It is only in this way that we can help those sections of the economy which need help the most, that is, the small borrower, the independent businessman and the farmer, for whom today there is not adequate credit available.
Again we come back to the principle that this government actually lays down in its policies, those principles which affect the nation's monetary policy. While we hear so much about inflation today, the truth of the matter is that there is not too much money in the country. There is an inflation in prices. As this comes about there is a lack of money in the country and the section of the economy which needs help the most is not getting that help. Therefore we would say to the minister that it is essential that this section of the economy be our concern.
The banks today, Mr. Chairman, are not facing bankruptcy. Their facilities are the best in the land. All you have to do is to note the new buildings and the improvement in banking facilities which has been brought about over the last few years. Likewise, their profits are among the best in the country.
This does not mean that the banks should not operate at a profit. They should. It does not mean that we are not in favour of private banking. It is the best form of banking ever devised so far as the private sector of the economy is concerned. But it does mean that we must protect those areas of our economy which are not able to protect themselves and which do not receive at the present time the protection and justice they deserve.
If Canadians really believe in free enterprise, they must see to it that the financial institutions are allowed to operate in an equitable atmosphere of fair competition. But on the other hand, just by raising bank interest rates we are not going to make the operations of these sectors of the economy as equitable as they should be. Today some small businessmen, including farmers whom I know pay up to 24 per cent on money which they cannot get through the private banks, money which I think it is the responsibility of private banking to supply in addition to supplying the capital needs of big business and industry.
However, to oppose this resolution as it now reads would be irresponsibly because it simply states that which must be done. It does not state what is the actual policy of the government. Again I would urge the Minister of Finance-and I think he would receive the support of the house-to permit the subject matter of this resolution to be referred to the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs so that we can really get down to the hard work of discussion and hearing the necessary witnesses so as to arrive at what I described as the highest common denominator of agreement.
There are several other points of importance, Mr. Chairman. I should like to refer to the Porter commission report which has been called a dead report; at least, it seems so. However, there are a few important recommendations made by the commission which we may be in danger of forgetting.
Again here I must emphasize the need of some form of control over the near-banks. The British Mercantile and Trust Company collapse, after the failure of the Atlantic Acceptance Corporation, makes this an urgent question which has yet to be dealt with and which I trust will be dealt with as we go through this legislation.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
What we need in Canada today is a desirable economy. Banking is the means by which this desirable situation within the economy

July 7, 1966
Bank Act
can be reached. I believe a desirable economy may be expressed as an economy which utilizes all modern methods oi production but which at the same time offers equitable employment tor all. I believe there is a national inventory of purchasable production which, when maintained by effective demand, would bring about a desirable economy. Effective demand is that which places in the population's hands the necessary purchasing power to buy those things that are necessary to make possible the standard of living of which we are capable, while at the same time solving the problems of distribution presently facing us. It is in this area, Mr. Chairman, where banking as it relates to the supply of money and to the supply of capital, which it is so imperative to have and which is actually the responsibility of the banking system, that this legislation is involved.
Finally, I would say that we must return to the part of sanity so far as our financial policy is concerned. The basic reforms which are talked about as being essential in our banking system are twofold. A permanent money supply is needed to cope in quantity with all sorts of needs. It is needed as a medium of exchange. With our tremendous potential in Canada and our tremendous know-how, there is no reason why our monetary supply for our monetary needs and our capital should not be adequate to develop to the limit that which we are willing to work at. Also, our financial system should be one that will distribute incomes to large numbers of our citizens so that everyone can have a certain reasonable standard of living quite apart from whether or not our citizens are able to obtain employment.
Again this comes back to a satisfactory money policy. I believe it is imperative for our banking legislation to be such as to provide for the supply of the public or social capital with which we have to build our bridges, schools, and hospitals. This is not capital which makes a profit, but it permits the development of the public sector of the economy without our having to pay the high rate of interest that we talk about in relation to the private sector where profits are permissible. Unless our banking legislation will permit the creation of that capital, and unless we can meet the needs of the people in supplying the required medium of exchange necessary to move, economically, that which we produce within our economy, an unnecessary burden will be placed on our people.

Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we again urge the minister to make sure that the subject matter of this resolution be referred to the committee where it can be discussed in appropriate detail in full debate.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in the remarks made by the Minister of Finance in bringing forward this measure the other day. One must realize that as he spoke he was thinking back to what has happened in this country during the past several years and what is happening today. The Canada of today is very much different from the Canada that existed when this government came to office a few short years ago.
As we look at the remarks which the Minister of Finance placed on the record we realize that the actions proposed in connection with the revision of the Bank Act are heavily influenced by the conditions existing in Canada at the present time, which the minister and other members on the government side have referred to as abnormal. These conditions prevail not only in Canada but also in the United States. It is interesting to hear the Minister of Finance of this country proposing that we bring forward legislation to meet an abnormal condition but which will have a long-term effect on the nation as a whole.
I come from an agricultural constituency where new industries are being developed today and, as in many other parts of this country, we know what tight money is. I say to the government that raising the ceiling on interest rates under the Bank Act will not solve the problem of tight money in this country.
Reference has been made to the arguments put forward by this country's banks which say that they have a problem with respect to lack of money. One of the reasons why the
July 7. 1966

banks have this problem is the utter failure of successive governments to deal with the consumer finance companies of this country which today operate under scarcely any regulation. Let us take a look at the over-all situation.
The banks tell us that all the money they have is in circulation. The finance companies take up the balance of the lending field. Raising the interest rate simply will not by itself solve that problem. What is needed today is legislation to deal with the finance and other consumer credit companies of this country. Such legislation would save our people some of the money that the Minister of Finance proposes should be expended on higher interest rates.
One need only look at the increased cost of housing, of development and of almost every other factor in our economy to realize that if the resolution is passed, as the minister explained it in his speech the other evening, this nation faces an increasing spiral of costs such as it has never known in the years gone by. At the present time this government has the reputation of bringing about the highest cost of living in the nation's history. Apparently the government now wants the nation to have its highest interest rates in history, which will lead to an even higher cost of living. For these reasons I cannot see how any thinking member of the House of Commons can support this resolution before us.,
There are other aspects I cannot possibly deal with in the short time available to me which have to do with the economic prospects facing this nation and also with our relations with the other nations of the world. Those nations demand that the action proposed by the government opposite be not taken at this time in our history.
For the last few days the Minister of Finance has been going around with a long face. We on this side and some hon. members on the other side of the house cannot help but know why this is so. The minister himself must have serious doubts as to the seriously detrimental effects that this legislation, if put into effect, will have on the economy of this nation now and in future.
Those who put their money into deposits should not expect the same returns that people who put their money into development are entitled to expect. The government and the minister suggest that we should pay a bonus to the person who is cautious, who is afraid to go out and try to develop this 23033-464
