nation. That sort of thing is almost a denial of everything that we in this nation believe in. Another effect this legislation will have will be to attract tremendous amounts of money from across the border, which is something that hon. members opposite seemed to be worried about in the months gone by.
When a home owner pays close to $20,000 for his home and the rate of interest he has to pay is increased by 1 per cent, he is immediately faced with having to pay approximately an additional $200 per annum. Taking the amount he has to pay over a 30-year period it can be seen that the additional cost the home owner has to pay is more than the total cost of many homes built in years gone by.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
We cannot but realize that this government not many months ago brought in amendments to legislation concerning farm credit which permitted an increase in the cost of credit to the farmers of this country. If the measure now before us were allowed to proceed there would inevitably be an increase in the cost of credit to those in the agricultural industry desiring credit for development.
But the man who cannot escape the consequences of higher interest rates, the man who cannot pass the cost on, is the man who carries a dinner pail. He, together with all those on fixed incomes and all those who must live on small incomes, has no redress. Once again in the measure before us we find the government loading down the man who carries the dinner pail with an additional charge on his income and one which he certainly cannot afford at this juncture in our history when Canadians are facing the highest cost of living ever known in exchange for the privilege of having a Liberal government.
I cannot but feel that regardless of where hon. members sit in this house, if they are to do their duty as protectors of Canada's financial soundness and her place in the world and help to provide a future for our citizens in their desire to earn a decent livelihood, they have no choice but to vote against this measure.
I believe the banks of this country have been doing a worth-while job. Today they boast, and we should take this into consideration, that they have made all the funds at their disposal available to the people of Canada for their use. If we study their

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-208, to amend the Crop Insurance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during the debate on the resolution stage of this bill I outlined briefly the current position of crop insurance in Canada and the roles of the federal and provincial governments in this important agricultural policy. At that time I indicated that I would go into more detail on the actual amendments when the bill came before the house for second reading. The intention in these amendments is to make crop insurance more attractive to farmers and more widely applicable to the risks of nature over which they have no control.
One of the basic problems has been that for large areas of Canada policies which are possible under the act in its present form do not appear to provide enough protection to the farmer. I am confident that these amendments will do much to rectify this situation and to make crop insurance universally more attractive and useful to Canadian farmers. The amendments to the Crop Insurance Act which you have before you make three major changes and two relatively minor ones in the current legislation.
At the present time the act authorizes the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces for crop insurance programs where the coverage does not exceed 60 per cent of the long-term average yield of the crop in the area. Many farmers, particularly those in areas where severe losses due to adverse weather conditions are not common, have felt that a coverage equivalent to only 60 per cent of the long-term average yield for the area was not in fact useful to them. Their position very simply was that they were good farmers and that seldom if ever did their production fall below this level.
Crop Insurance Act
The proposed amendment, by increasing the permissible level of coverage to 80 per cent and by permitting the calculation of the average yield on an individual farm rather than an area basis, is designed to provide protection commensurate with each farmer's needs and with his ability as a farmer. The proposed 80 per cent level is a maximum level. Policies could be sold at any level of coverage up to 80 per cent. Obviously, however, the higher the level of coverage under any given circumstances the higher must be the premium rate. A condition of the legislation is that the premiums, including, of course, any payments made by either this government or a province toward this cost, must be such as to make the program selfsustaining.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The second major amendment increases the premium share payable by the federal government from the present 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the total premium. Let us assume that the premium rate for an insurance policy is $1 per acre. Under the current legislation the farmer pays 80 cents and the federal government pays 20 cents. Under the amendment the farmer will now be required to pay only 75 cents, with the federal government paying the remaining 25 cents. This action should go some distance in reducing to the farmer the costs that will be associated with the upward movement in the level of coverage. It means that farmers across Canada taking out policies under this program will, on the average over the long term, receive a return of $1 for every 75 cents they pay into the program, since 50 per cent of the administrative expenses are also paid by the federal government and in all agreements to date the other 50 per cent is paid by the province concerned.
Under the existing legislation the coverage is limited to crops. Thus what might loosely be called production units such as apple trees or stands of perennial forage crops cannot by themselves be covered. Yet losses of these production units can have very severe and far-reaching effects for producers. In the case of fruit trees, not only does the farmer lose the crop for that and several ensuing years but he suffers direct financial loss in having to replace the trees that have been lost through adverse weather. A parallel situation exists for many other crops including certain long-term forage stands.
Another and somewhat similar problem exists in the case of summerfallow. In certain

July 7, 1966
Crop Insurance Act
areas land that has been summerfallowed during the previous year with attendant costs accruing to the operation sometimes cannot be seeded because of excess moisture. The amendments make provision for coverage for losses of this kind. For this extended coverage, as it is called, the amendments authorize the making of contributions by the federal government equivalent to those made for crops per se.
Two minor amendments are included. The first of these alters slightly the deductible amount payable by a province under the reinsurance scheme. Under the present legislation the deductible, that is, the amount that must be paid in indemnities by the province before the federal reinsurance becomes operative, includes the premium receipts for the year, reserves from past years and an amount equal to 2J per cent of the total liability of the province under policies in force. The amendment reduces the deductible amount payable by the province by the amount of any reinsurance premium that it may have paid in that year. This is considered necessary since, because of the method of payment of the reinsurance premiums at the end of any insurance year, the amount of money in the fund for the payment of indemnities has been reduced by the amount of reinsurance premiums paid by the province.
Under the present wording of the act a province with no reserves for the payment of indemnities would be in the position of having to pay an amount equal to the reinsurance premium from its own resources together with the 24 per cent deductible before the federal government would share in the cost of further indemnities.
For the success of any program one of the most important features is that its users understand it fully. This was clearly brought out during the resolution stage of this bill by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchin-ski) who indicated that there was great need for more information on the program at the producer level. Accordingly, the act is also being amended to provide that agreements with provinces specify the manner in which policyholders are informed as to the benefits accruing to them because of participation in the program.
During the debate on the resolution stage of the bill the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) asked why the experience of P.F.A.A. had not been fully utilized in the development of crop insurance. He also asked for assurance that P.F.A.A. would not be discarded or the act revoked at the present

time. The experience of P.F.A.A. has been used extensively in the development of crop insurance programs. The yield statistics and the administrative experience of the P.F.A.A. organization have been available and continue to be available to any province to assist in the developing of their crop insurance programs. In addition, the present director of crop insurance is a former director of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. He is thus able to bring to the development of crop insurance the knowledge and experience gained by that organization in a period of 25 years.
I agree with the hon. member for Medicine Hat that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should remain in effect until such time as experience has given farmers an opportunity to judge the relative merits of crop insurance and P.F.A.A. for themselves. I suggest to the house that we can depend on farmers to indicate by their participation in crop insurance programs which of these measures, in their opinion, offers the most useful protection.
In summary, then, the amendments increase the maximum permissible level of coverage from 60 per cent to 80 per cent, permit coverage on the basis of individual farm yields as well as area yields, increase the federal contribution to premiums from 20 per cent to 25 per cent, and permit coverage for fruit trees and perennial plants.
These are amendments which I am confident will result in a most useful and workable crop insurance program being made available to Canadian farmers.

Crop Insurance Act
We welcome the introduction of this legislation in the house, since it merely supplements the one we had proposed ourselves while in power. We give our hearty support to the improvements that will be made in the existing legislation. If I meant to be nasty,
I would avail myself of this opportunity to say that the hon. minister has stolen a plank from our platform, since before the November 8 election, one of our electoral slogans was the improvement of the Crop Insurance Act so as to make it more readily available to farmers.
As the minister wishes to take advantage of such an improvement, we heartily support his efforts and hope the legislation will be enforced as soon as possible.
For a certain group of farmers, this measure is extremely important. In order to show the importance of crop insurance, I would just like to recall the two hail-storms that affected recently my constituency as well as that of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pilon). As to the havoc created in my riding, in the sole parish of Saint-Pie de Bagot, many farmers have seen the efforts of many months of work completely ruined.
Crops of farmers cultivating beans, peas, tomatoes, com, strawberries and even tobacco were heavily damaged on the evening of June 17 last. For instance, the bean crops of 35 farmers were affected and the assessment of the damage is between 80 and 90 per cent, while the damage to the acreage varies between four and 40 acres. These figures give a clear idea of the damages.
When crop insurance will be put into force, it will surely be a relief to the farmers who are at the mercy of the vagaries of weather.
Another disaster also struck the orchards in one part of my riding as well as in the riding of my friend from Chambly-Rouville, as I said earlier.
I have here a brief sent me by the secretary of the Societe Pomologique et Fruitiere du Quebec in which it is stated that 5,300 acres of orchards were damaged by the two storms on June 14 and 17 last. Representations are now being made to get subsidies from the federal and provincial governments.
Even if crop insurance were put into force immediately, the farmers and the apple growers concerned would suffer heavy losses.
Before closing, I would like to ask the minister to whom I wrote to receive favourably the representations which will

Mr. Speaker, I am sure everyone will be interested in the proposition contained in this amendment to the Crop Insurance Act which has already been amended once since it was originally passed. It was passed in 1959 and amended in 1964. It is now being amended for a second time in a major way.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) can perhaps learn a lesson from the two pieces of legislation which he recently brought into the house, namely, the so-called $4 milk policy and this piece of legislation. In both cases there is the presupposition that the federal government has no jurisdiction in this field but that jurisdiction must be exercised by the provinces and that the federal government should hold out to the provinces a carrot which is large enough to provide an incentive to the provinces to do something about the situation.
I am aware of the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) during the election campaign last year indicated to the farmers, particularly in Timiskaming where he started his campaign, that the federal government was going to solve the problems we were experiencing in that area where there was an almost total agricultural disaster as a result of weather conditions. Hay had been lost, and this was followed by the loss of a large portion of the grain. In some areas almost a 100 per cent loss of hay and grain was suffered by the farmers.
The promise made at that time was that assistance would be available as soon as it was asked for. A hasty retreat was then beaten because this request could only come from the provincial government. The minister of agriculture of the province of Ontario told the farmers there were so many disaster areas in the province that if the riding of Timiskaming, which is almost identical geographically with the district of Timiskaming, were declared a disaster area, numerous areas throughout Ontario which were seriously affected would also ask for assistance and the province of Ontario would not be able to pay its share and assistance would not be forthcoming.
July 7. 1966

[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
If there had been an insurance program in effect it would have covered the major cereal crops as well as the forage crops in Timis-kaming. In addition, it would have looked after the drought areas in Renfrew and eastern Ontario. These farmers would have found themselves in a position of being able to ask for fairly sizeable payments as the result of the provisions contained in the bill before these amendments were introduced.
There is an indication that such an insurance program as Is being undertaken by the federal government will probably be a good thing, but whether or not provincial governments will be able to conduct a successful crop insurance program that will be within their means is something else again. The situation in Timiskaming, in my opinion, has been drastic. It has been drastic in other areas and not merely because of a disaster in one year but because of the cumulative effect of disasters over a period of years. The Minister of Agriculture is well aware of the situation because of conditions in his own area over a period of time.
If we pass this legislation we are again asking the provinces to do something. We are adopting a philosophy that has been apparent in Canada, particularly when governments want to adopt it, of saying that something lies within provincial jurisdiction but at the same time passing overriding legislation in other areas. The minister mentioned P.F.A.A. I was interested in the detailed investigation of P.F.A.A. which occurred when the officials of that organization were here. They were asked whether recommendations had been made for the extension of this type of program all across Canada and in other fields. They have had a fairly good record in western Canada of preventing disasters at what we in Ontario would consider a reasonable cost. I am referring to those areas in particular where there is not a one-crop economy.
In the riding of Timiskaming a farmer will put about one-third of his farm in hay. There will be a considerable acreage put into hay and quite often it is allowed to go to seed. We have been producing about half of the timothy seed in the province of Ontario during the last two years. A great deal of the farm land in the area is put into either hay or seed production. Another one-third of the area is put into mixed grain and the remaining third is usually put into ensilage or temporary pasture which will be broken up in the fall. Therefore in the area there is a variety of
Crop Insurance Act
cereal production as well as forage crops.
This production is augmented by several other cash crols such as corn, potatoes and vegetables.
I have found that when farmers have discussed crop insurance they have discussed it in terms of the total crop. I am pleased to note that Ontario has taken steps to bring forage crops under their crop insurance scheme. However, if a farmer insures hay he will probably find the cost is more than the risk warrants. If he insures corn the same condition arises. If you are feeding beef cattle or dairy cattle and you are not operating your farm for off-farm sales but as a production unit, you can cut some of your grain for forage if your hay crop is a failure.
You can increase the amount of grain you feed your cattle and probably utilize the straw. Therefore the loss that you would suffer in total agricultural production would not be exceptionally great. For this reason the farmer feels it does not pay him to insure these crops. In the last three years in Timiskaming, particularly last year, what happened was that some farmers had a total loss. They did not get any hay and they lost their total grain production. They were not even able to get any straw that would cover their need for bedding material. The loss for these farmers was almost total; yet to guard against this loss they would have had to insure the grain, the forage crops and probably the pasture as well. The cost, therefore, is not sufficient to warrant the carrying of this type of insurance.
I believe the federal government has a responsibility in this area. What amuses me is the fact that we say we have jurisdiction in one field and yet not in another. I do not consider the prairie provinces to be a provincial unit. They still have representation on a provincial basis individually. I believe, therefore, that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act did take into consideration the fact that these were three provinces for which the federal government was able to provide crop insurance on a limited basis. If it was possible to have jurisdiction to enact the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, it should be possible also to enact a crop insurance program. I believe the reference to provincial jurisdiction is an excuse for not implementing federal legislation.
I would be very happy, Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Agriculture would decide to enact a crop insurance program that would cover all the provinces of this country, and let the

July 7, 1966
Crop Insurance Act
Supreme Court declare it ultra vires. I know the province oi Ontario is not going to challenge the legislation because that government has been plagued ever since it thought of a crop insurance program in trying to find a program the farmers would support. I believe it is fair to say this program will not get the support of 50 per cent of the farmers. This is not an indication that 50 per cent of the farmers in Ontario do not need crop insurance. I think it is safe to say that about 90 per cent of the framers in Ontario are in desperate need of crop insurance that will allow them to count on at least the 80 per cent return which it is within the statistical ability of the crop insurance program to provide. I should like to see a real shuffle in the federal government in terms of the legal advice it receives. I know that when four or five constitutional lawyers get together you will get four or five different points of view. [DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
I should like to see an action with respect to the matters I have raised brought before the Supreme Court. Sometimes, however, it makes little difference what happens in the end result because the problem usually crops up in a different way next time.
We must face the problem of providing the type of insurance that is not tied entirely to payments made to a provincial agency. We shall have to operate this program on the basis of income. The crop insurance will have to be in terms of the income that is involved in the crop. I believe that there are ways in which this can be done.
I am sure the minister will agree that the insurance premium will not be collected as easily as if one were to levy, say, one cent per bushel going at the elevator or by doing it under any system similar to P.F.R.A. It will not be that easy. No matter whether the agricultural commodity involved is hay, feed grain, seed or any other crop that is handled as a direct sale, or whether it is something that comes from a farm production unit such as beef, poultry, swine or any of those commodities involved in the field of milk production, a percentage system based on the price of sale of those commodities I think could be worked out to enable the premiums to be paid as the sales of the end products are made. In this way the program could be universal and could be applied to all farmers.
I know that the Department of Agriculture will not recommend this. As we have heard in the committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development, the department has had

considerable problems in making arrangements in various fields of farm endeavour to get farmers registered in the various programs. I suggest the program would further complicate the department's problems immeasurably.
I am concerned that those in my area who need insurance most are the ones who can least afford it. It may be true that many farmers cannot afford to have this program if they have to insure a number of commodities. It is easy if you can insure one particular crop such as wheat, hay or corn. That is particularly so if you are in an area that is involved with only one particular commodity. I am sure this is true around Delta and in some of the southern ridings where tobacco is grown.
I suggest to the minister that the program will not work better now than before but that it will be extended to an additional number of farmers. What we are really doing is holding out a carrot not to the farmer but to the provincial governments so that they may implement this sort of program.
I have been critical of crop insurance since we first passed the legislation because I do not think it is universal and because I do not think it can be universal, not because the farmer does not want it but because he thinks he cannot afford it and that it is not designed for his particular need.
The federal government having raised its contribution, I think it is worth while to bring under the Crop Insurance Act fruit trees and perennials. They are found in limited areas in Canada and are a one-industry crop. It will not be difficult to insure crops in these areas under this act. The amount of money involved in losses and the amount of money that will be demanded as a premium by the provincial government will probably make this program feasible in those areas. They will benefit from this sort of insurance, and I am very pleased that this amendment has been included in the over-all amendments to the act. This amendment will be beneficial and is an answer to the requests of associations that have come before parliamentary committees in the past asking for this extension. These associations have shown us the unique problems of one industry areas that are dependent on one very perishable dommodity.
I would be remiss in my duty, Mr. Speaker, if I failed to ask the minister if he has taken into consideration a bill I have on the
July 7. 1966

order paper which will be increasingly important in this field as days go by. The bill proposes to the Department of Justice and other departments the national licensing and regulating of rain-making equipment. I should like the minister to draw an inference from what happened in his own area of the country. For several years the Renfrews were plagued with a very serious drought of long duration. The provincial government as a last resort, and it will admit it was a last resort, brought in rain-making equipment. I can remember being in the Ottawa valley at fair time. I am sure most members agree that the weather in southern Ontario is at its best at that time. Most of the fairs, including many little fairs in the Renfrew area, were rained out because of not only minor showers but torrents of rain. The farmers of that area not only had drought for four or five months throughout that year but because of the intervention of the Ontario Department of Agriculture they were deluged with rain in the latter part of the season. So they had two disasters in one year.
I admit I am exaggerating but I am raising the matter so that hon. members may consider this proposition. If the federal government undertakes to cover disasters with crop insurance and allows agencies not connected with the Department of Agriculture to interfere with the elements and bring about disasters, it will have to pay the losses caused by such disasters. I can remember the tears that were shed last year when we wanted to adjourn the house to discuss this matter.
There is some indication that we can interfere in a limited way with the elements. We may find ourselves, on the one hand, agreeing by government action to a situation with regard to which, on the other hand, because the elements have been interfered with, we have agreed to pay compensation. It is a little like saying that we will insure all the houses in an area that are burned down but we will not get rid of the arsonist in the area who is burning everybody's houses. You cannot insure the house if you cannot take care of the man who wants to burn it down.
I have raised these matters because I think they must be considered. I do not know how many farmers will take advantage of this program. It is very hard to put a figure on the damage that might be anticipated through natural causes and it is very hard to extend the liability to damage brought about by other causes.
Crop Insurance Act
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
The minister showed considerable initiative. At any rate, shortly after his appointment he was brave enough to take on the C.P.R. With a temperament of this type we would expect him to encourage the federal government to give more positive leadership in fields such as crop insurance and not to content itself with providing substantive legislation as a basis for action by provinces which may desire to make use of it in a limited way. We are paying a large percentage of the money and the provincial governments get the credit. At least under P.F.R.A. in days gone by the federal government got the credit and, moreover, used the patronage machine to great advantage. Today this aspect of the legislation has grown less important and it may be more of a liability than an asset.
Today we should look at these things from a national point of view and ensure as far as we can that real initiative is taken by the provinces, many of which are now unwilling to assume liability. In Timiskaming last year we, like other parts of Canada, were facing disaster conditions and very often farmers were unable to cope with the situation. As a result farmers in my area had to borrow money to buy seed. Germination from the corn harvested last year was less than 10 per cent. They had to obtain bank loans to buy hay which cost as much as a dollar a bale. I know that similar conditions existed in the Ottawa valley. I say we must provide more positive protection against disasters of this type than we have in the past.
As I say, I support this legislation because I believe it is creeping in the right direction. But I hope the minister will come back to parliament in the fall after considering this matter with the other agricultural ministers of Canada and present to the house a much more extensive form of insurance which will take into consideration not only the loss of crops but the income farmers receive from the sale of their products. If he does this I believe he will receive the support of most members of the house as well as the backing of all farm organizations for bringing into being a program which is likely to prove much more equitable to all concerned.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION, EXTENDING OPERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has touched on many of the points I had intended to raise. First, I should like to teU *he minister how pleased I am

July 7, 1968
Crop Insurance Act
that there is at last a policy to extend crop insurance to the eastern provinces. This program enabled western farmers to survive in a great many instances when they needed help, though I still have some hesitation about its application generally.
I was glad to learn that the ceiling is to be raised to 80 per cent. Crop losses in western Canada cannot be assessed on the same percentage basis for purposes of insurance as those in eastern Canada. Losses incurred in eastern Canada seldom result in a yield going below 60 per cent. Nevertheless they can be disastrous. Western farmers too must be pleased with the higher ceiling and with the provision which is being made to cover a wide field of farm production, including both raw products and modified products.
It is true there are many products that need to be covered. One is feed grain which is sold to nourish dairy cattle, beef cattle, poultry and swine. In the eastern regions of Canada there are a great many varieties of farming while in western Canada, at least in the prairie provinces, production is limited to beef or grain. In British Columbia fruit growing is important. There are a great many orchards in Ontario and in Quebec as well as in the Maritimes. In the Maritimes large crops of potatoes are grown and this crop too should be covered by the insurance program.
I do not know exactly which agency in Quebec will deal with this plan. So far I do not believe there is an agency in existence. But I shall be watching to find out how this process works. The federal government will be handing out money to the provinces to cover the losses incurred by farmers and, as the hon. member for Timiskaming mentioned, I certainly hope that without unnecessary interference in provincial affairs the administration here will keep a watchful eye on the manner in which these moneys are dealt with.
I have been a witness to some of these federal-provincial goings-on. The provincial authorities had a high hand in them but when it came to helping those who needed help there was a little favour shown to one and a little disfavour to another, or what we commonly call patronage. This should not be the case. If this is a public insurance plan no consideration should be given to political affiliation. When a farmer suffers from crop failure he needs help and usually he needs it immediately, not in three or four years time. A farmer in eastern Ontario seeds in the spring and in all likelihood he needs the

money from that crop to pay his debts. Some farmers have been waiting for a year or more for back payments on dairy products. If there is to be a similar delay in handing out crop insurance payments the prospect is an unhappy one. It may be said that payment will be made eventually. But in the meantime farm creditors are pressing and farmers cannot wait that long. For this reason I hope payments under this scheme will be made as quickly and as fairly as possible.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Another difference between agriculture in eastern Canada and western Canada is the price per acre paid for land. In the east farms are smaller and prices tend to be larger, though, of course, there are high prices and low prices. Production on the farms of eastern Canada, particularly in Quebec except for the Richelieu valley, is largely confined to poultry, swine, beef cattle and dairy cattle. Wheat and grain production do not amount to much because the land is not suitable for that purpose. The farmer has to depend on pasture and forage, and if crop insurance does not cover all these things it is useless to him. As the hon. member for Timiskaming said, the purpose of crop insurance is not to make money on it. Its purpose is to help a farmer get through a bad year without going into debt. As matters stand now, if some mishap occurs many farmers have to leave that industry.
In my own region there are some poor farms. Beef cannot be raised on stones. These farms are useless for growing crops or hay. Even mountain goats would have difficulty surviving on them. But some good farms in the area have closed down because of crop losses. I hope the provincial government of Quebec will expedite its legislation and work in co-operation with the federal government. Farmers must be helped in many ways whether they are engaged in the production of beef, swine or feed grain. If a farmer loses his hay crop and has to import feed at high price from a distance he may as well stop farming, considering the price he gets for his cattle today.
Judging by the energy the minister has displayed I am sure he will do his utmost to provide a better standard of living for the agricultural sector of the economy and without discrimination between east and west. Western Canada has appreciated crop insurance for some years, but the program will have to take into consideration different factors in eastern Canada where farms are
July 7, 1966

smaller and there is a greater variety of production.
I hope the minister will keep a vigilant eye on the provincial governments to see that they do not start fooling around with the funds given by the federal government. I hope the provincial governments will not delay in making payments to farmers in distress. If they do delay the farmers will have gone out of agriculture completely.
The remarks made by the hon. member for Timiskaming about rain-making machines caused me to smile because he said the provincial Department of Agriculture in Ontario sort of ordered things about to get rain. The former minister of mines and natural resources in Quebec, Mr. Rene Levesque, authorized the placing of these machines and I know that where he did there was plenty of rain. One year the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) swam around his constituency, and the same thing happened in Lac-Saint-Jean.
I do not know how good these machines are but I do know that where they were operated plenty of rain fell. In fact, where previously we had a drought we ended up with a flood. Both conditions are equally bad. There should be some control over the use of these machines in order that they will not produce more damage than they are designed to prevent.
When payments are made under crop insurance I hope they will be just and honest without taking into account a farmer's political affiliations, and I emphasize that last point because in the past there has been some discrimination. We look forward to the passage of Bill C-208, and after it has been in effect for some time and experience has been gained in its administration we shall look forward to future amendments to the legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION, EXTENDING OPERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the minister's answers to some of the questions I raised when the resolution was being discussed. I know that some of the people in the department have had a great deal of experience in the administration of P.F.A.A., particularly one official, and what I would like to know is whether the minister and his officials gave serious consideration to expanding P.F.A.A. so that it could provide a measure of crop insurance.
The $800 maximum that is available now certainly does not cover even the basic cost of putting in a crop on most farms, and of
Crop Insurance Act
course it is not applicable to all the areas in Canada. But with the experience which the personnel of P.F.A.A. have in its administration and the data contained in office records, it seems to me the government could have moved into crop insurance in a better way than by having each of the provinces plow new ground in trying to develop a satisfactory crop insurance program.
The minister has not indicated whether serious consideration was given to extending P.F.A.A. into other areas of Canada, increasing the levy presently being imposed on farmers, including other products in addition to cereal grains, and increasing the benefits provided. Crop insurance is essentially a plan to provide payments to remove the element of tragedy or disaster resulting from the loss of a crop in any one year. It is not intended that payments be large enough so that farmers would find it profitable to operate under crop insurance. In 1939 payments under P.F.A.A. were as low as $300. They now go up to $800 but, as I said previously, this does not cover the cost of putting in a crop. But it does provide that the farmer does not have to go on municipal relief.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
If they have crop losses year after year such as happened in one part of my constituency for seven years in succession because of hail storms and so on, then even with the assistance of P.F.A.A. it is necessary for the provincial and municipal governments to provide additional service. I will just leave that for a moment. I am pleased to support the part of the bill which changes the coverage from 60 to 80 per cent.
In clause 3 there are amendments allowing the amount of the insurance to be effective on any crop in an area, or on any farm in the area. It is to be based on the average yield of the crop or on the farm, whichever is the greater. I suppose the details of administering this part of the amendment to the act will be left up to the provincial government and the provincial crop insurance administration. However, I should like to point out that there is a really serious administrative problem here in trying to establish what the average for a crop may be on a single farm experience. When the act will say from now on, if this bill passes, that it is permissible to issue insurance and to pay benefits on a single farm experience, it is not clear to me how this is going to be arrived at. Are we going to ask the farmer to keep records? That is.

July 7, 1966
Crop Insurance Act
one way to determine what the average crop may have been for that farm.
It seems to me in this regard that we might be entering an area where losses in yield may fall within the category of losses over which a farmer had some control; in other words, he might be following poor farm practices. If he were able to buy insurance based on the average for that entire area, which naturally would include a number of farmers who practiced proper husbandry and who had reasonably good crops year after year, his would be a farm unit within a whole group which would be able to obtain insurance at the same rate as his neighbours who were practising good farming methods. Almost continually every year he would be collecting insurance.
I do not see anything in the federal act which prevents this kind of abuse. I raise this point because I know in certain parts of Saskatchewan, and even one or two places in Alberta, charges have been made that there are farmers who simply farm for the dry bonus, the P.F.A.A., and scratch in a crop in the spring without any particular diligence in so far as seeing that a good job is done, because they can collect P.F.A.A. in the fall. I am not saying this practice is widespread, because I do not think it is; but there are a few, and this irritates the good farmers who are around them.
Unless I am incorrectly interpreting this part of the bill, any farmer may buy insurance at the same rate in an area based on the average yield of the area or the farm, whichever is greater. If the average for the entire area is greater than the average for his farm, a farmer will be able to buy insurance up to 80 per cent of the average for the area. There probably are cases where an individual farmer may have been unable to produce 50 per cent of the average in the area, and if he continues that kind of practice, then he can collect 30 per cent every year.
I think we should be a little more careful and not allow this kind of abuse to creep in.
I suppose when the minister replies he is going to suggest that the provincial crop insurance legislation and administration ought to be set up in a way which would prevent this happening. But, Mr. Speaker, so far as the federal legislation is concerned this is permissible. I think this is something we should be careful about.
There is another point I should like to mention to the minister and the parliamentary secretary. In a number of statements the

minister has indicated that the federal government apparently is rather anxious to expand crop insurance to as many areas as possible, and very quickly, so that it will be unnecessary for the federal government to move into an area with emergency assistance in an emergency year. Because of the problems involved in working out the details, we come to a situation where we have a federal crop insurance scheme in respect of which it is unfair for the federal government to try to force crop insurance at an accelerated pace by withholding assistance for emergency purposes. I do not believe that a crop insurance program is something which can be forced.
I would hope that the pilot projects which now are operating in Alberta, and to some extent in Saskatchewan where they have been in it a little longer, and even in Manitoba, will not be forced to expand because of this kind of attitude. There will be agricultural years, not only in the prairies but in many other parts of Canada, when there will be disasters due to weather, drought, flood, hail frost, or other reasons. I think the federal government should be disposed to co-operate with the provincial governments in taking care of these emergencies without holding up the crop insurance program and saying that it will take care of these things, because up until now six out of the ten provinces have not even tried it at all. Even in those areas where there have been pilot projects going for some time, both the provincial departments and the farmers concerned are not satisfied there is sufficient experience to say that it is entirely satisfactory.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I just wish to say that I think we are a long way from having worked out all the details of a completely satisfactory crop insurance scheme, taking into account the variations in climate, soil conditions, and also the many products that are produced in Canada. Therefore, I would hope that we do not try to move too quickly. I would hope also that we do not disregard programs such as P.F.A.A., which have been satisfactory in the past. I should like to see some change of attitude; that is, a recognition that the federal and provincial governments have a responsibility to deal with emergencies when they arise. I should not like to see it suggested that we are going to withhold this because we want to get crop insurance in as quickly as possible. If there was some kind of near perfect scheme, near perfect bill, and near perfect administration in existence at
July 7, 1966

the present time, then I think there would be some justification for this attitude. In the meantime I do not believe it is fair to force on provinces or municipalities some kind of an alternate scheme to meet emergencies, in view of the fact that these schemes are far from perfect at the present time.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up a great deal of time, but I do wish to say that I am pleased by the amendments now before us. Perhaps I am in a somewhat different position from the three preceding speakers, because in the late 1940's I was instrumental in urging Manitoba farmers to press the provincial government to carry on an examination of the possibility of adopting a crop insurance program. As a matter of fact, I owned a grain farm, and I spent my winters travelling through the province encouraging farmers to take some action. As a result of the action taken the provincial government set up a commission in the early 1950's to study the whole question of crop insurance.
At that time I had made some examination of the programs that were in existence in the United States. I presented a brief on behalf of the farm organization to this commission, in which we recommended certain things in respect of a crop insurance program. That commission quite rightly recommended that a crop insurance program be set up, but only if there was federal assistance made available. No such assistance was forthcoming from the Liberal party, which was in office until 1957.
In 1957 this party assumed office and that year a bill was presented and enabling legislation was passed. In 1959 the province of Manitoba embarked on a crop insurance program on a trial basis. Test areas were set up throughout the province in order to gain the experience necessary to implement a crop insurance program which would be successful.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) went to great lengths to point out the need to go slowly on this measure. As a matter of fact, the government of the province of Manitoba has urged these amendments on the federal government because in its experience it feels they are necessary in order that it may expand its crop insurance program to cover more crops, giving a wider range of coverage.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I did not say that the federal
Crop Insurance Act
government should go slowly in dealing with these amendments. I suggested it should proceed slowly and cautiously before extending crop insurance to areas where it has not existed before. I am sure the hon. member wants to be fair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION, EXTENDING OPERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I accept the hon. member's explanation of what he intended to say, but his explanation does not make sense, because in the final analysis the provincial government requires this legislation in order to adopt or enlarge crop insurance programs. This decision rests with provincial governments, and rightly so. The provinces must decide what crops should be covered and what areas should be covered.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) was advocating a national crop insurance program on the one hand, while on the other complaining because farmers could not participate in existing programs. If they cannot participate in a program that has been developed by a provincial government to suit a province's needs, surely it is unreasonable to expect them to participate in a program that is supposed to have national application. The experience that is necessary for the development of crop insurance programs must be gained in particular areas where the crop insurance is to be applied.
I do not wish to assume the minister's task of explaining some of his comments, but because of my experience-I happen to be one of the few farmers in this chamber who has participated in a crop insurance program in my province-I do know something about crop insurance and I should like to make a few comments.
I cannot follow the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, who suggested that P.F.A.A. should be expanded in relation to a crop insurance program. At the same time, he complained that farmers in certain areas were taking advantage of P.F.A.A. by sort of dipping their fingers into the till. If we enlarge the provisions of P.F.A.A. to cover crop insurance across the country, we would be creating a greater opportunity for this sort of thing to take place.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat also complained that certain farmers may not be following good farming practices, yet would benefit to the same extent as others. He suggested that some provision should be adopted to prevent this from happening. Under the Manitoba crop insurance measure

July 7. 1966
Crop Insurance Act
there is a provision which allows the Manitoba crop insurance corporation to exclude any farmer from coverage if it is felt he is not following good farming practices. In the final analysis the determination as to whether or not a farmer is going to participate in a crop insurance program must be left to the farmer himself. This is one of the strongest arguments against a nationally applied insurance program. Only by looking at insurance rates applicable in certain areas and by considering crop prospects can a farmer decide what type of crop he is going to grow, and whether or not it will pay him to take out crop insurance. For that reason and many others the type of program that was developed in 1959, now being amended, is the type of program that in our experience in Manitoba works to the best advantage of the farmers, and those people charged with the responsibility of administering it.
This bill provides that summerfallow will be eligible for insurance coverage. This was not so in the past. Again I do not wish to take credit for the adoption of this principle, but I must say that for years I urged the Manitoba provincial government to adopt this type of amendment. In many instances in my area the farmers were not able to seed crops because of excess moisture. That is one condition that could arise to prevent the seeding of a crop. It is rather difficult to apply this type of insurance to second year crops because one has no way of knowing whether or not a second year crop can be sown. Even at this time, when the amendments are now before us, there has been a change in respect of summerfallow. This is the result of improved marketing conditions for grain. Many farmers now are not putting any land in summerfallow, but because of reasons beyond their control they are going to be in the position, of not being able to collect insurance if they fail to seed a crop in a particular year. In this area perhaps the minister will have to project his thinking further. I am not criticizing the amendment-I think it is a good one-but we have reached the point where we should consider action on a larger scale.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
There can be no objection to the raising of the coverage from 60 to 80 per cent. However, I doubt very much there will be many farmers on the prairies who will wish to participate in a program on such an increased level of coverage. In connection with that, I should like to ask the minister a question with which he might deal in his statement. I wonder whether he could supply us with

figures in regard to the increase in the premium rate when the coverage is raised from 60 to 80 per cent. In other words, could he tell us what are the premium levels at the present time and what they will be in the future. I am sure his officials have done some calculations on this matter and can provide us with the answer.
So far as the intention of the federal government to increase its participation in the premiums is concerned, again they are behind the times because the 5 per cent increase in the federal government's contribution to the premiums has already been swallowed up by the application of the 11 per cent sales tax on farm machinery, by the increased interest rates which will accrue as the result of the recently stated intentions of the government, and by the increased cost of living. And so the farmer gains nothing from this 5 per cent increase, although the minister may try to take credit for doing something that is supposed to have some appeal.
I was rather amused at the reply which the minister gave to some previous observations which were made during the resolution stage of the bill. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you allow me, I should like to make a few remarks regarding Bill No. C-208.
Crop Insurance Act
Coming from a mostly rural riding, it is only natural that, like my colleagues, I should be interested in a legislation designed to improve the Crop Insurance Act. Considering the several disastrous years we have experienced lately, especially with regard to agriculture, of course, our interest in this bill is quite understandable.
I know that other members who do not share my political views, had the opportunity to speak at the resolution stage. Going through Hansard for June 21, I found that some members from Quebec were prevented, for lack of time, from showing their interest in the matter.
A few, last minute items of information make it possible for me, first of all, to congratulate properly the Minister of Agriculture for his interest in a situation which surely deserves our fullest consideration.
Obviously, the improvements which will be brought about will be a valuable contribution to the output of our farmers. I knew for a fact that Quebec-I am referring to the administration which has now been superseded-had indicated its intention to introduce crop insurance in the province of Quebec, but no legislation had yet been brought forward to implement such a hope entertained by so many of our farmers. I am convinced that with the increasing and imperative consideration agriculture requires, the new administration will also examine the problem. Meetings such as we witnessed today, between the federal and the provincial Ministers of Agriculture bode well for certain agreements. Some aspects of Bill C-208 have especially interested me, namely section 3, subsection (2), paragraph (fa) which reads:
-specify the manner in which the province will inform each person to whom a policy of crop insurance is issued of Canada's participation in the insurance scheme under which the policy is issued; [DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
This is one more commendable step which I support readily; it might do away with the goings on that have occurred too often in the past where, under joint programs, the federal government unfortunately did not get the credit it deserved in the case of similar legislation. This happened not only in my province but also in others where the provincial authorities have used such legislation to their sole benefit. I believe this provision

July 7, 1966
Crop Insurance Act
will convince our constituents that their representatives in Ottawa-which we call at home the far-off federal capital-consider at least the problems which face them.
This increase from 20 to 25 per cent of the federal government contribution in respect of the premiums is praiseworthy. I trust that when circumstances allow in the future, and with the blessing of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), the contribution can be increased again perhaps, so that more help may be given those provinces which are less fortunate than others.
I also notice, with regard to extended coverage, that it is stipulated in clause 5A(l)(b) as follows:
-loss arising when the seeding of summer-fallowed land intended to be used to grow an insured crop is prevented by excess ground moisture, weather or other agricultural hazards.
I did not have time to discuss the matter at length with the minister, but several weeks ago I had the opportunity of advising him in writing of a rather special problem, in my riding at any rate, with regard to the fairly extensive damages caused each year, and even twice a year, to fodder crops by migratory birds on their arrival or departure, on the islands in my riding and especially on the south shore.
The problem is this: we have, and with reason it goes without saying, laws protecting migratory birds, which laws were introduced by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing). Migratory birds are of great importance to the economy of my riding which is always in need of help, like many others of course. We want to protect the Canada goose, but if our farmers' crops are devastated completely when the birds swoop down on their fields, or on the strand, the farmers should be allowed to include those losses under the crop-insurance program. I am thinking in particular of the inhabitants of the islands whose crops are more severely affected by what constitutes, after a fashion, a devastating pest.
Of course, looking at it from the standpoint of sports, particularly during the hunting season in the fall, we are always pleased to welcome, for the greater part, our neighbours from the surrounding constituencies, from the city constituencies, even people from Montreal, and in particular the many Americans who, each year, have the good habit of hunting migrating fowl in our area. Then we are faced, if you want, with measures to protect

that sector of our economy, but also to handicap it. I would be very pleased if this item was included in the improvements to the Crop Insurance Act, in order to kill two birds with one stone or two good birds with two stones, if you will, Mr. Speaker.
The reason I took part in this debate was simply to thank those who had the excellent idea of making further improvements to this act. We know that a first improvement will open the way to others, and I dare hope once more in concluding these brief remarks that the new administration which took over in our province, will carry on with the good intentions at least shown by the previous administration to introduce, as soon as possible, in the province of Quebec, which, I am convinced, surely needs it, legislation with such an important scope in the interest of the agricultural class, which was unfortunately neglected for too long and not sufficiently assisted.
I hope these few remarks will be taken into consideration, and I wish to assure the minister that, thanks to the assistance and the valued advice his department will provide us with, and mainly the information that the Department of Agriculture will be pleased to forward to us occasionally, we will be able to become happy and particularly skilful propagandists who will succeed in selling the idea to a greater extent in our province, so that the Quebec farmer may benefit from legislation which will be entirely to his advantage.

I am prompted to rise, Mr. Speaker, because of the remarks made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson). It seemed to me that in his handling of this subject he really illustrated the hesitancy that has characterized the lack of action of the government of Alberta. He remarked that, this legislation is far from perfect; that he was afraid that in the event the farmers had insurance they would not be able to come to the government for help in case of disaster; that he did not consider the scheme feasible as it is now. All of these remarks, Mr. Speaker, are occasioned by what I believe to be a fundamental failure to grasp the general idea behind this measure.
Of course it is not perfect. This is a new field. We do not have a model or a pilot program because of the varying climatic conditions and the different crops grown in
July 7. 1966

Canada. It was thought the most feasible insurance scheme that could be worked out would be one worked out by each province, cognizant of its own conditions and problems. The federal government therefore merely provided the vehicle by which they would co-operate with the provinces in any scheme that the provinces developed. The federal government would share the cost, allowing the provinces, because of their special conditions, to develop the scheme. Certainly if the hon. member for Medicine Hat had paid any attention to the idea behind the development of the scheme, we would not have heard the speech that we did hear. It is left to the provinces to develop the type of insurance scheme, the type of coverage best suited for that province. The scheme might only cover certain areas or certain crops; it may only be taken a certain distance and the province would find that would be about the limit of the practical coverage needed.
The whole idea was that the scheme would have to be developed by the province itself. I say the attitude of the hon. member for Medicine Hat is reflecting the slowness of our own provincial government in Alberta, which only last year started to take a tentative look at this act. They should have been developing ideas as they have been doing in Manitoba for the last four or five years, and by now we might have a substantial number of farmers receiving some benefit from this act. I cannot for a moment imagine how the hon. member could use the argument that these farmers, having been covered by insurance, would be unable to ask for aid in case of some disaster. He is probably referring to the number of times that farmers, because of drought or flood, have had to come to provincial and federal governments, hat in hand, and ask for special grants. I suppose that is a nice position in which to have the farmers. Certainly I cannot understand the hon. member's failure to realize the number of minor tragedies -minor because they are isolated-where the losses suffered by individual farmers would be alleviated by insurance. These are instances where it is not a serious enough matter nationally, perhaps even provincially, for the provision of any other source of aid.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
I do not want to take any further time of the house, but I do hope that the province of Alberta might go to the province of Manitoba now, find out what they have learned, perhaps receive a lot of good help from them, and be able to make up for the last three or
Crop Insurance Act
four years which the province has wasted by not developing this scheme. They should start right away, as are other provinces, to develop a crop insurance scheme which would be of considerable benefit to the people of the province.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are two or three questions which I believe were pertinent and appropriate. I am afraid I cannot answer all of them because there are not complete or absolute answers to all of them.
The hon. member for Provencher asked a question with respect to the increase in premium by increasing the coverage from 60 to 80 per cent. I believe that was the question about which he was exercised. There is no categorical answer in this regard. It depends, of course, on the nature of the area being covered.
As hon. members know, the agreements with the provinces will prescribe the particular divisions of areas which are made, and alternatively, as conceived in the bill, this could even be on an individual farm basis. If a province, in its wisdom, saw fit, that would be an applicable method. The increase in the premium will depend on the nature of the area, the crop and the losses in the particular area. But certainly the increase from 60 to 80 per cent indicates a very considerable increase in coverage; and, like any other form of insurance, you pay for what you get.
I am sure that many farmers will find that the 80 per cent increase in a particular area which is growing a particular crop will be more than they wish to pay. I do not think that all of them by any means will want to buy an 80 per cent coverage policy. However, under the scheme they have the chance to buy even lower than 60 per cent coverage if they so wish.
I regret that I cannot give any categorical answer to this question. I am informed that in a high risk area, with probably a high risk crop, the difference between 80 per cent coverage and 60 per cent coverage could

July 7, 1966
Crop Insurance Act
involve as much as double the premium; but
this is merely an illustrative figure. Certainly the cost would be higher, and in the case oi many crops it may well be that the farmers do not wish that type of coverage.
Judging from the many discussions which we have had, the added coverage is particularly attractive to growers, such as fruit growers, tomato growers and people engaged in these areas, where a 20 per cent loss represents a very serious loss. They are the ones who particularly require this coverage. I regret that I cannot be more categorical, but to the best of my knowledge there is no absolute answer to the question posed by the hon. member, except that which we will gain from experience.
The hon. member for Cumberland posed a question as to whether Nova Scotia is more likely to participate in crop insurance as a result of the amendments. My instructions are to the effect that, as a rule, when the maritime provinces suffer a loss it is not complete or total. Apparently the sovereign province of Nova Scotia enjoys such a salubrious climate that this type of complete catastrophe does not occur too often, or as often as in agricultural communities in other provinces.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, at the federal-provincial meeting which was held last February, I believe, to determine the directions in which the various provinces wished to move in the area of crop insurance, the officials from Nova Scotia indicated that the 80 per cent coverage in particular was of great interest to them. This is the specific aspect of this bill that seemed to indicate that it would be of interest to them, and that it might encourage the province of Nova Scotia to make further inroads into the area of crop insurance. I take it this is probably because of the fruit growing areas there. Since that time we have had no further indications as to what are the intentions of the province of Nova Scotia in this regard.
With regard to the hon. member for Medicine Hat, I am not going to give him a hard time, as did the hon. member for Ed-monton-Strathcona, but I will try to answer one or two of his questions. He was concerned that the premium structure might be conceived on an area basis, whereas the amount payable on loss would, on the other hand, be returnable on a farm unit basis. I may not have made that too clear in my original presentation.

This could not be the fact. The premium
structure has to be conceived either on one basis or the other. Either the premium structure in the provincial agreement may be on an area basis, in which event the loss ratio or risk in the particular area is calculated actuarially and both the premium and the return in the event of loss are based on an area basis, or alternatively, if the provincial agreements so prescribe, the coverage may be on a per unit or per farm basis, in which case the premium is calculated on the risk for that particular farm unit in light of the number of years required experience. The loss is then based similarly on the premium paid. In other words, you cannot have it both ways. Either your premium is based on an area basis, in which event so is your loss; or your premium is based on an individual farm unit basis, and so is your loss.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
I might point out that this latter incentive in the act may not be achieved in all provinces overnight. It may well be that before a premium structure can be conceived on a per farm basis, some considerable experience is going to be needed before an actuarial calculation which is meaningful can be arrived at. But the aim toward a per farm coverage is, I think, a very desirable one, as pointed out by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, in that this will be the ultimate encouragement to the individual who is a good farmer and has an efficient production. He can insure his own farm according to the productivity and risk of that particular unit, which in the case of the efficient and productive farmer costs obviously less than if he insured on an area basis, where he may have to take some less efficient farmers in with him in the calculation of the premium structure. So, I think the hon. member points to the ultimate idea, namely a per farm coverage on an experience of a sufficient number of years determined adequately and actuarially, which will enable the good farmer to buy his coverage more cheaply than if he were less productive.
I do not need to tell my friend, who is extremely knowledgeable in this area, that this matter has been one of the complaints with respect to P.F.A.A. The good farmer pays in and never collects, and the others take money out almost every year. Twenty five years out of 27 I think is the record. This is the reason for having this matter within the ambit of this statute, so that ultimately coverage can be made on an individual basis. Such coverage will be most economical for the
July 7, 1966

effective farmer, and it will encourage
efficiency, because efficient farming will lead to a lower premium structure. In very much the same way, if you have not had an accident for 25 years driving your car, and if nobody under 25 years old drives your car, your insurance will be at a much lower rate than it would be if you were a high risk.
I might also remind the hon. member that the premium structure has to be approved by the provincial government, and therefore here we have to safeguard to the effect that the premium structure, when conceived under any agreement, will be sound actuarially. As a result greater participation in this scheme will be encouraged.
Those, I think are the major questions of which I have made a note, Mr. Chairman.

The point I was trying to make is that we need the broadest possible flexibility with regard to coverage of fruit orchards in particular, a (8:20 p.m.)
I understand there are many people who have small orchards which do not represent their total income, but which is additional to their income. The rest of their income may be derived through other farming, or through work in industry, and they may have a few acres in fruit trees. Such a farmer may not wish to have as expensive a coverage as someone who depends for his entire livelihood on fruit trees. Therefore, I think the widest choice should be available so that the man who does not wish to buy comprehensive coverage may have available to him a more limited coverage at cheaper rates. He may not want coverage which is as expensive as that required by someone who is depending on the crop for next year's living. I believe the widest choice should be made available to the people.

It is one thing to have an act and another thing to administer it. In this regard I think the minister will run into one of the greatest problems he ever has had in enforcing an act. What does excessive ground moisture mean? I can see the minister as a lawyer in a court room developing an entire case around what is excessive ground moisture. To me this phrase is very wide, and should be narrowed down much more than it is.
I also feel that if you are going to give crop insurance to people with summerfallow, and it is flooded over one year, probably because it has not been properly tiled, and then the next year it is flooded over again, that man should tile the land. Is he entitled to insurance? I think this will be very difficult to enforce. We speak of fruit trees. How will their value be established? They may be

young trees, half-bearing, or full-bearings trees. I think there is a real problem for the department in this.

Mr. Chairman, I have no doubt there will be problems. One of the small mercies within all this is that I will not have to administer it. It will be administered within the ambit of the insuring authority in the provinces. Again this is an attempt to broaden the scope of the act to enable the making of agreements which will give coverage in mixed farming areas in respect of fruit trees and forage crops which has not previously been available. In all fairness, and without taking anything away from the western farmer, I think I should say this act probably was more beneficial as previously drawn in respect of a one-crop farm, such as that which produces wheat.
The province of Manitoba used the act as it exists very extensively, and this was very encouraging. This is an attempt to break new ground in an area where up until now it has been thought that it would be too difficult to insure. Such being the case, I think undoubtedly there will be problems such as are envisaged by the hon. member. It must be remembered that in any particular area this must be actuarially sound; the losses must be covered by the premium structure. Certainly the insuring authority, be it a board, commission, or whatever administrative agency is created to administer the program, is going to have to assure itself that this scheme is acturarially sound.
With regard to the coverage involving excessive ground moisture, I think the policy itself likely will have to spell this out specifically. I believe we run into the same thing with a fire insurance policy which covers water damage. The arbitrating authority has to determine whether this is water damage caused to the items which are covered under the policy.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Certainly I am not trying to minimize in any way the difficulties or problems that will have to be faced in making available policies that give coverage for such things as excess ground moisture and an appropriate interpretation by the authority which will determine the loss-that of course will be the insuring authority-but I feel sure this measure will give an opportunity for broader coverage than presently exists.
While I feel very certain there will be difficulties such as the hon. member has

July 7, 1966
Ways and Means
envisaged, I do believe this measure will make coverage available on a sound and effective basis. In early years of coverage I am sure there will be some problems in respect of forage crops, and that there will be some people who will feel that the coverage has not been what it should be. This always happens in respect of insurance. However, I do believe that this is the only way we can give an opportunity for coverage, particularly to eastern mixed farmers to whom it has not been available before, because the act was not sufficiently broad.
I am not minimizing the difficulties envisaged by the hon. member, but I feel confident we will be able to work these things out and thereby afford a wide choice of coverage on a premium structure which will be advantageous to many areas of agriculture which are now not covered under the act.

One of the departments covered by the bill is Veterans Affairs. There is a great deal of concern in the minds of many veterans because they will not have the opportunity of speaking about a certain problem following the passage of this bill, in view of the fact that it covers the total appropriation for the Department of Veterans Affairs.
The problem to which I refer relates to something we have been talking about for several days, the old age pension increase. Certain veterans feel that an increase in old age pensions will be granted in some provinces through the passage of supplementary legislation by provincial legislatures, and that 50 per cent of that increase will be paid by the federal government.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Of course this will be fine as far as it goes, but I am told that the veterans have already been informed that if they receive this supplementary benefit as the old age pension increase, then their war veterans allowance will be reduced by the same amount. It seems to me a very sad state of affairs that the Department of Veterans Affairs should send out this notice on a nation-wide scale to compensate for the information which has been disseminated by another federal department through the provincial election machinery, all of which is not normal procedure. I think it has been generally agreed by all members in this house that veterans allowance is a reward for services rendered, that it is not gratuitous but that it is deserved by the veterans. This payment is made under very strict conditions and in a limited number of cases.
Ways and Means
I should therefore like to know what remedy the Minister of Finance, or maybe the Minister of National Revenue, will apply to correct this situation in which provinces pay an additional supplement to the old age pensioners, and the veterans affairs department reduces the payment made under the War Veterans Allowance Act by a similar amount.
We have always tried to maintain the pension structure in such a way as to keep pace with the payments in other sections of our social security program. In my opinion the veterans of this country should not be the ones to be unfairly treated. For this reason I should like to receive some information regarding the intentions of the government in dealing with this problem, and an explanation of the stand taken by the Department of Veterans Affairs according to which the supplementary payments made by the province are deducted from the allowances of the war veterans. I do not wish to belabour the point, but I think it should be raised and answered because I think it is doubtful, unless pension legislation is introduced in this session, that there will be an opportunity to raise this matter.
This may be one of the reasons for the reluctance shown by the department in passing the estimates before this situation is clarified. I think veterans all across Canada should be assured that if there is any advantage to be gained from the additional amount being paid by the provinces, which I understand approximates $25, $12.50 of which would be paid by the government, this amount should not be reduced from the war veterans allowances.
What this measure means, in my opinion, is that the ceiling of the allowances which the war veterans collect is changed, old age pension and other forms of aid being included as income. They should therefore be assured that this limit will be raised sufficiently to allow the veteran the benefit of living in a particular province where this extra payment is made.
