I cannot allow this opportunity to pass, Mr. Chairman, without trying once more to bring before the government the sorry plight of the agriculture industry and the trouble it is having with the gap between the cost of production and returns from the sale of products. I should like to dwell for just a moment tonight on the fact that men who have been engaged in this noble industry are selling their farms for whatever the market value may be, and going to the cities with their families to try to obtain employment in whatever fashion they can in order to provide a living comparable to that of their neighbours. I am very much concerned that here, in the province of Ontario as in the other provinces of Canada, we find men leaving the land in ever-increasing numbers.
Tonight, I should like to dwell for a few moments on the troubles of the dairy industry. I do not wish in any fashion to display partisanship in relation to this subject, but to point out as honestly and fairly as I can some of the major troubles facing this industry. Certainly the government should be concerned over the fact that in the last 10 months that there have probably been dispersed, principally in Ontario, as many valuable dairy herds as in the preceding five years. Certainly something is terribly wrong when these men put on the market blood lines that are the results of perhaps two or three generations of concentrated work. The same thing is happening in the poultry industry. In the last three or four years perhaps half of the small producers of eggs in the province of Ontario have gone out of production. They no longer produce eggs even for their own consumption, because they feel it is no longer economic under the conditions that exist today.
These are not the so-called marginal and submarginal farmers; these are professional farmers. These are good farmers. These are

July 7, 1966
Interim Supply
farmers whose family enterprises were the pride of the neighbourhood. What is wrong? Why are farm delegations approaching every provincial capital and the federal capital in the hope that some assistance of a financial nature may be forthcoming to relieve them of this terrible burden? I have before me a small table from which I should like to quote. It has been compiled by the Ontario Milk Marketing Board and I think, in some small measure, indicates what is wrong. I know there are many figures that can be cited pro and con. I know there are figures to show that dairy production units in Canada are receiving ever more money for their produce. These figures are available. However, the fact still remains that farmers are not receiving enough money to cover their expenses. These are figures put out by the Ontario Milk Marketing Board and they show that in the period 1955-65 the price received by farmers per hundred for milk has gone up 17 per cent. I believe it has. However, please note that in the same period farm wage rates rose 54 per cent; farm machinery prices increased 46 per cent; taxes and interest rates were up 58 per cent. The composite index for farm required goods and services rose 36 per cent. We do not need a mathematician to calculate that when this happens there is bound to be trouble in the industry.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
There have been discussions in the house and questions asked of the Minister of Agriculture about his new dairy policy. There is no doubt in my mind and in the mind of every man in the industry that this government did try to do something to help the dairy industry. In other words the government was familiar with the problem which existed. But it has been found-I think there is general agreement on this on all sides of the house-that under the very workings of this policy not every farmer will get an average of $4 per hundredweight for his milk; this is not going to happen.
I would point out that the very report of the minister himself, whether intentional or not, and the advertisement carried in all of the trade papers in the field of agriculture across the country, led the milk producers to believe that they would receive a return of $4 per hundredweight for their milk. I should like to quote one of these ads put out by the Canadian Department of Agriculture, Ottawa, under the signature of the Minister of Agriculture. In large headlines it states:
The new federal price support benefits all milk producers. Average return $4 per hundred.

On reading this, any dairyman would be of the opinion that he is going to receive $4 a hundred average return for his milk. When he does not receive that price, even though you tell him to read the fine print or put up any alibi you want, whether it is right or whether it is wrong, the farmer concerned will be of the opinion that the policy is not working for him.
I should go on to read the fine print because I know the Minister of Agriculture would wish me to do so in order to be perfectly fair. It states:
The federal government, through export assistance and direct purchases of such products as butter, will create a demand which will enable processors to pay $3.25 per hundredweight of manufacturing milk with a 3.5 per cent butterfat content.
I must be absolutely fair to the Department of Agriculture and the minister, because I point out that it goes on to say:
However, the government has no authority to set the prices processors pay producers. It is in your own interest to negotiate the best possible price for your milk through your farm organization.
That statement was made and perhaps it is the fact. However, the fact still remains that when the government asserted that the factory would pay the farmer $3.25 per hundred for his milk, and that the government subsidy of 75 cents a hundred would bring the price up to $4 average to the producer, every producer of milk felt that that was true. But when he goes to the factory and does not receive $3.25 for 3.5 per cent butterfat content, but only receives $3.08, or $2.95, or $2.60, his arithmetic soon tells him that adding 75 cents to that price cannot give him the prescribed $4 per hundred, and he feels he is being gypped. He feels this program is not giving to him what it promised him, and if that is the case then something is drastically wrong.
I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that if this policy is not being and cannot be administered so as to guarantee $4 per hundred, then the headlines of this advertisement should not have been worded in this fashion-that the new federal support benefits all milk producers and gives an average return of $4 per hundred. I maintain that this headline is misleading. The department that administers this act has assumed that the average price paid to the producer of manufactured milk will be $3.25 per hundred and that a subsidy of 75 cents will give them $4.
It is very easy to go to every farmer who produces milk and explain small details. The federal government says that the guarantee
July 7, 1966

of $3.25 lies within the purview of the provincial governments. The whole program is based on a price of $3.25 f.o.b. factory. This is where we run into the greatest difficulty. The federal government says that the provinces should see to it that the price is $3.25. The provincial governments say that they have no right to ask for an additional subsidy because this would create unfortunate competition between provinces. They say they cannot guarantee a price of $3.25 by legislation. The provinces say that because the federal government is paying a partial subsidy and promoting the price of $3.25, jurisdiction lies within the federal government.
The farmer does not care which government has authority or where the responsibility lies; they know that they are not getting $4 per hundred for their milk. I agree with them that something is wrong. That is the kind of policy which is driving the farmer off the farm. What the farmer needs is dollars, and they cannot get them by unfulfilled promises, misleading advertising or from quarrels about jurisdiction. The time has come when this policy must be changed.
I was very encouraged yesterday to learn in this house that there was going to be a meeting between the ministers of agriculture of Ontario and Quebec and the federal minister to look into this question. I think that this is a step in the right direction. This is where we have to act. We must work as a coordinated body not as individual segments. In this way the farmers themselves will have more of an opportunity to express their views and influence the governments.
This meeting of minds is nothing new, Mr. Chairman. This is the program which was initiated in 1961 when we were the government. We felt that since Ontario and Quebec were the largest producers of dairy products in Canada, the only method from which we could derive a system whereby the producers would receive a fair return was by having a uniform policy with both the provincial governments and the federal government playing their part.
The provincial government of Ontario-and I must give them credit for this-carried out their part of the agreement and tried to establish through the Milk Marketing Board a price of $3.25 per hundredweight f.o.b. factory. Unfortunately in the province of Quebec, instead of the government then in power establishing this price which had been agreed upon, it turned to a policy of direct subsidization of 35 cents per hundredweight
Interim Supply
in the wintertime and 17J cents per hundredweight in the summertime, which threw the whole arrangement out of gear. It just could not operate in that way.
Yesterday, as I pointed out, we were encouraged by the fact that the minister of agriculture of the new government of the province of Quebec, as well as the minister for Ontario and the federal Minister of Agriculture are returning once more to the federal capital to look into this entire dairy program and into the reason that it is not paying $4 per hundred or more to the primary produces.
It is my hope that since he has a second chance the Minister of Agriculture will convince his colleagues that the policy which he has enunciated in its present form will not, and I maintain cannot, achieve the goal they were satisfied it would achieve.
I think that the ministers acted in good faith and were sincere in their belief-and I must give them credit for this-in advertising to the farmers, the primary producers, that they would receive $4 per hundred. But, Mr. Chairman, as a result of representations both outside the house and inside the house and from the provincial governments concerned, they must surely be convinced that other steps must be taken to guarantee the floor price of $4, which no one in this house on either side has, to my knowledge, has said that the farmers should not have. There seems to be unanimity of opinion in this regard; everybody feels that the farmers are entitled to this price.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
My request to the government tonight is that it look at this matter in its proper perspective, that it make its own inquiries into the industry, and that it sees to the farmers getting what they want. The farmers who bring their problems to us are satisfied that they will not get what they want. And how is that, Mr. Chairman? How do they know they are not getting what they want? By the simplest and most positive way that I know. When they get their cheques in their hands, those cheques do not add up to $4. If the cheques do not add up to $4, then this is not a good policy. Farmers are not considered, whether the matter falls within provincial or federal jurisdiction. All they know is that they are not getting $4. My sympathies are with the farmers, Mr. Chairman.
Now that the minister has had an opportunity of learning what the problem is from

the ministers of Ontario and Quebec, who are closely associated and connected with this matter and who are constantly meeting with members of the dairy industry, I hope that he has learned that the formula devised by the government is not working. I hope he will devise ways and means of achieving the objectives that all members of this house wholeheartedly desire, namely that the dairy farmers receive a minimum price of $4 per hundredweight.
It is to be hoped, Mr. Chairman, that the National Dairy Commission, as introduced by this government, will in 12 months have had an opportunity of achieving its desired purpose of administering the entire dairy industry in Canada.
In conclusion I want to say this: My plea tonight was on behalf of the dairy farmers. Every other segment of industry in Canada today is in a terrible economic squeeze, and something has to be done. Mr. Chairman, something has to be done now. Farmers face increased prices on everything they buy; they face increased taxes, higher labour costs, higher prices of farm machinery, and they are facing a desperate strait. When I see in my own neighborhood dairy herds that have been established for two or three generations being indiscriminately sold on the market because the family no longer thinks that it is economically feasible to keep those herds, there is something terribly, terribly wrong. As mentioned by the hon. member for Oxford, these herds are being exported out of the country. They are not being bought by neighbours, friends, or anybody going into business. They are lost to us.
I am sure the government can quote figures showing that the situation is not as bad as portrayed, and that production is almost the same as one year ago. The increase in production has been slightly under 3 per cent. This increase in production is caused by the fact that farmers are selling the less productive animals and keeping the more efficient ones. Farmers are deperate, trying in every way possible, by additives to feed, by fertilizing pastures and by a varity of methods, to increase production per annum in a desperate attempt to survive. This maintenance of production, as in many other sectors of the country, is not permanent. It is only temporary, because it is the last ditch stand of Canadian agriculture. Unless help comes from the provincial or the federal level this country will be importing all its food at a very high cost, to the shame of those men respon-

sible for the collapse of this once great and proud industry.

That was a nice speech, Eric.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Thank you.

May I answer this question? The fact remains that the quarrel about provincial and federal jurisdiction is of minor application in the field of policy. The federal government states, and I believe correctly, that within the law it cannot establish a price at any level, whether it be f.o.b. the factory or f.o.b. at the front gate of the farm. At least, the government cannot do this without going into the field of provincial jurisdiction. Perhaps this is so.
On the other hand the provincial governments claim, I think equally correctly and equally within the law, that if the federal government is taking measures under the Agricultural Stabilization Act to promote a price which this act says may be paid, but not "must be paid", then they will not accept the same degree of responsibility as they should.
If the government is providing a method of maintaining a price to the farmers by having legislation saying that it may, will, or can establish a price, but not saying it shall or that it must, the division is too fine, and the farmer understands only that he has got a certain number of dollars in his pocket. That is the attitude he takes.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say, as I should have said when the resolution was introduced, that the resolution is with respect to interim supply in the amount of $1,662,982,791.93, which will carry us through to October 31, 1966, and deals with all departments other than the departments which were just previously approved by the House of Commons, with respect to expenditures for the current year.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot let this opportunity pass without expressing my disappointment about the dairy policy of the present government.
When the minister announced the $4 per hundredweight policy, he assured us that all farmers would receive that amount. And even today we are still trying to make him understand that some farmers, or most of them, are not getting and will not get those $4. And in spite of that I notice that the minister seems convinced that the farmers who are not getting those $4 are probably to blame because, as it was said this afternoon in committee, if the producers, the processing plants do not pay the amount of $3.25, the farmers should bring some pressure to bear on the processing plants to get it.
That, Mr. Chairman, is an answer which surprised me greatly coming as it did from the minister. And he tells us to clear himself that the setting of the price by the plant is not a matter of federal jurisdiction. He is right about that. But such is not the case at all when he publishes in all the newspapers his announcement to the effect that from now on farmers will certainly get $4 per hundredweight for their manufacturing milk.

And we are trying to prove to him-besides we have the evidence-that right now in my region it is impossible for the farmers to get those $4. As a matter of fact, I have here the photostat of a document showing the amount paid to a farmer; he gets exactly $2.86 per hundredweight plus 75 cents added to that. That is far from the $4 guaranteed by the minister. That is for one plant only and it varies from plant to plant.
Well, I say that the minister spoke to the newspapers to get some publicity. It would have been much better to say: We are just giving 75 cents and we are not responsible for the rest; we do not guarantee anything and it is impossible to guarantee anything because it is a matter of provincial jurisdiction. Once again you are getting into a provincial field. Therefore you cannot guarantee anything. All you can guarantee is 75 cents. Why not say it and then you will not get all the farmers mixed up. Just say: We are paying 75 cents. It remains for the provinces or the farmer associations to reach an understanding with the plants to get the best possible price.
Thus, you will not disappoint a whole region. The farmers tell us: They promised us $4 and look at what we are getting. It is not what they are getting now which is abnormal but the promises, the advertisements which have warped the farmers' views.
I wish to say to the minister tonight that we have proofs and that he must have some too because there have been complaints.
I have here the periodical La Terre de Chez-nous dated June 29; it is the organ of the Catholic Farmers Union, the largest farmer organization in my area. It states that the milk policy of Ottawa is inadequate. That is clear. It is inadequate. In this publication, the milk policy is discussed on two and a half pages. I shall not impose the whole thing upon you, but I shall read the significant parts. On the front page, it says:

On that occasion, the members of the executive committee were informed that a meeting with the Minister of Agriculture in Ottawa, the Hon. J. J. Greene, produced no practical results.
Well, that is factual, sir. They came, they stated that they had obtained no practical results. It was then unanimously resolved to send a telegram to the Minister of Agriculture. The telegram was published in the

Mr. Chairman, if these statements are not proof of the discontent and dissatisfaction of the Quebec farmers, I wonder what the minister is waiting for to at least try another survey and, for that purpose, the minister must first of all recognize that the farmers are not getting and cannot now get $4 per hundredweight.
I think the minister will have to meet again with the organizations, because if a price of 75 cents per cwt. is unsatisfactory, another basis will have to be established. If it is truly wished to help the dairy producer, he cannot be left any longer in doubt owing to the prices being changed from week to week by manufacturers, processors or, at least, the minister should not say he wants to help the farmers. Nowadays, farmers are expecting action from governments. One thing surprises me on the part of manufacturers. I wonder whether it would be possible, during federal-provincial meetings or conferences between Ministers of Agriculture, to see to it that a processor is obliged to pay a certain price, if a minimum price is finally to be established for the milk producer. Otherwise, I feel that any federal reform on the present basis is absolutely worthless, because it is realized that as soon as the federal government offers a 20 cent subsidy or increase, manufacturers and processors reduce their prices by 20, 25 or 30 cents.
Consultations will have to take place at all costs so that farmers no longer will be the victims of such haggling. Mind you, I am not accusing the federal government any more than provincial governments, but I say that some action will have to be taken so as to urge milk processors to stop any such haggling with, and pilfering of the farmers by all sorts of means. The latter is being shortchanged on the butterfat content, in a word, he is being cheated in every way in an attempt to recover 10, 20, 30 or 40 cents. It seems to me that the various Departments of Agriculture, both provincial and federal, should come to an agreement to try and guarantee a reasonable price to our farmers so that not only would they no longer be exploited but could sell their production at a fair price.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to call this particular point-actually it is the one about which my electors feel most bitter-to the attention of the minister.
I do not know whether the situation is worse in Quebec than in the other provinces but, to my mind, the evil is widespread. According to some of the members on various committees, it seems general, and I do know that, as far as Quebec is concerned, all our associations are clamouring for help from the federal government. Let us start with something definite, then we can find out what the Quebec government can do in this respect.
One more word about the farmer to prove, in passing, that if Quebec farmers sometimes complain, they have a right to do so, because they are often treated most unfairly. We have proof of this in the report of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) on loans granted under the Farm Improvements Loans Act.
We have been saying for four years that when it comes to collecting taxes, Quebec is right there in the forefront, but when it comes to giving the people something in return for their taxes, then it is quite another story. In the field of loans guaranteed by the federal government, out of 46,285 loans made in 1964, Quebec has had exactly 873 compared to 1,224 in British Columbia, 13,528 in Alberta, 14,790 in Saskatchewan, 6,181 in Manitoba, and 8,473 in Ontario. And some claim that Quebec has its share, that Quebec is well protected. Well, if that is the general opinion, you can be assured, Mr. Chairman, that it is not the opinion of Quebec farmers. And the proof is there. Every time we can

obtain details, we notice such glaring inequities with regard to assistance to farmers, the other provinces come first and the Quebec farmers get only the crumbs.
Well, I suggest that the present Minister of Agriculture will have to look after the province of Quebec if he does not want to lose support of 100 per cent of its farmers because if things do not improve, we will urge Quebec farmers to look after their own needs, to withdraw their federal taxes and to look after their own business as it is no use counting on receiving help from the federal department.

Mr. Chairman, I quite appreciate the fact that hon. members who have spoken are most concerned with the problems of the farm community, as indeed am I, and as I am very certain the government is. I quite appreciate that in many respects the farming community has not kept abreast of the burgeoning income and very prosperous and buoyant economy we have enjoyed in the last couple of years.
It may be in the nature of things that when an economy expands very rapidly, when industrial wages and industrial prosperity grow up at the pace they have in the past two years of full employment, the farm community is slower to catch up than many of us would like. Hence I share the concern of hon. members opposite for the needs of the farm community, for the importance in seeing to it that we have policies which enable the farmers of this country to enjoy the very high standard of living and the great economic opportunity that have been afforded to their confreres in the industrial world in the past two or three years under this administration.
But, Mr. Chairman, I think we do little service to the farm community, and I think I know enough of the farmers now and the integrity with which they are prone to behave, if their case is misrepresented. I think we do the farm community the greatest service if we put their case on a factual basis, and I have every confidence in the rest of the Canadian community, and the Canadian public at large, that if we put the case of the farm community on a fair, honest and upright basis, other sectors of the Canadian economy do not wish to be subsidized by that farm community.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I do not think other Canadians would want the farm community to live at a lower standard of living than they do. I feel sure that if 23033-466 i

their case is put honestly and fairly before the Canadian public, the Canadian public would wish that the policies of government and otherwise would be such that the farming community would be able to enjoy every opportunity they enjoy in the other booming sector of the economy. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think it is incumbent upon me to set the facts and the record straight in this regard in the interests of the farmers of this country. I think that is the way they would wish it.
There has been some reference to the government's dairy policy. To the best of my ability I should like to set the record straight in this regard. In the first place, as has been said by many more able and better men than I, this is a very difficult country to legislate in in respect particularly to marketing legislation of any kind, by virtue of our constitution and the judicial interpretation of our constitution, especially the judicial interpretation of the constitution with regard to the farm marketing legislation made in the 1930's.
I think all would agree, as did the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) quite candidly, honestly and forthrightly, there is no power in the federal government to fix prices within a province. The other day I think the hon. member for Grey-Bruce read a portion of an article from the Canadian Farm Economics. Although I feel sure he did not do this deliberately-possibly it was because he did not have time to read it all-I believe he may have left some misconceptions on the record. He read from page 11 of the Canadian Farm Economics, volume 1, number 1, of April 1966, published by the Economics Branch of the Department of Agriculture. He read as follows:
The Federal Government has jurisdiction over the market for manufactured dairy products-
I believe the record indicates that that is as far as he read. I feel sure he would want me, in the interest of stating the whole picture correctly in Hansard to read the rest of the paragraph. That paragraph says:
The Federal Government has jurisdiction over the market for manufactured dairy products to the extent that products move interprovincially and into export markets.
I feel sure he would want me to add those latter words in order that the record be very clear that milk products of all kinds within a province are purely within the ambit of provincial jurisdiction.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we have had some representations by the hon. member who last

July 7. 1966
Interim Supply
spoke, and some inference by the hon. member for Kent, Ont., that the government's policy as announced and as advertised in some way misled or was intended to mislead. I should like to quote from my statement in this house when I enunciated the government's dairy policy on March 23 at page 3041 of Hansard. At that time I knew the interest of members opposite and knew that they would want to know exactly what this program was and how it would be carried out. The words I stated were:
The support level will provide for an average net return of $4 per hundred pounds-
As all advertisements have said.
-of manufacturing milk testing 3.5 per cent but-terfat content, basis f.o.b. the factory.
I cannot think of any way in which it could have been put more plainly than that. In order that there might be no misconception, no misunderstanding, and no delusions in this regard, I further stated as follows:
The policy will apply in general as follows:
For producers of manufacturing milk, the board-
This is the stabilization board.
-will take measures designed to permit processors to pay a price of $3.25 per hundred pounds for 3.5 per cent manufacturing milk. Direct payments to producers from the board of .85 cents, minus a 10 cent export assistance levy, will be used to bring producers' average net returns up to the $4 level.
Again, so that there might be no misapprehension and so that all members of this honourable house would have the policy as clear as crystal in their minds, I enunciated the following caveat:
However, the federal government has no authority to set the prices that processors pay to producers. I feel It is important, therefore, to stress that it is incumbent upon producer groups and boards to do all they can to see that this market price level is achieved.
I can think of nothing which could have been clearer than that. This is exactly what has happened and is what we have done. I feel sure that if hon. members wish to be candid about the policy, how it was enunciated and how it has come to pass, they will agree that we have done exactly what we said we would do, which was the only approach we could take within the ambit of our constitutional responsibilities.
Again, with regard to the needs of the farm community, let me make it very clear that this program means the farmers of Canada will get between 14 and 15 per cent more gross return for their milk, and therefore for

their manufactured milk, this year than they did last year.
Hear, hear.

I heard considerable comment from the other side with regard to labour wage settlements which invoked an alleged 30 per cent increase over a two year period. I think that surely on this side of the house we can be rather proud that even though these wage increases for labour were very appreciable we were able this year to give to the dairy farmers of Canada the same increase in the nature of 15 per cent. I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that this involves the spending by the federal government of some $90 million which again is a very very considerable sum. I think it is an indication of the concern that this government has for the farm community of Canada, for the eastern farm community of Canada which had been so badly neglected in past years, that it saw lit to establish at the federal level a program that would benefit the dairy farmers of Canada.
Again let me set the record straight by placing some statistics before hon. members of this house. When we talk about the price of farming products let us remember that in respect of the dairy policy of the federal government in the days when the hon. gentlemen opposite were in office, just as now, the government did the only thing it could do at the federal level; it set the price f.o.b. the factory. So, any recriminations which are coming now are rather hollow in the light of the fact that when the gentlemen opposite had the responsibility their policy was geared to this basis just as it always must be at the federal level.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Let us see what has happened in respect of price since we have been in office. When we assumed office the net return to the farmer for manufacturing milk at the farm gate, at the farm house, was $2.70 in 1960. It was $2.68 in 1961-not too great improvement in that year by hon. gentlemen opposite. It was $2.64 in 1962-down 4 cents. That was not a very good year for the eastern farmers when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office. In 1963 it was up one cent to $2.67. In 1964 it went up to $2.77, and last year with the supplementary payments it went from $2.77 to $3.26.
Hear, hear.

May I ask the minister a question?
July 7, 1966
I do not have much time and I should like to complete my statement.
The minister is misleading the house.

This year the price at the farm gate will average somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3.75 with an average transportation cost of 25 cents. This leaves an average price increase of 50 cents which is the highest in the history of this country.
I do believe that the records should be set straight. The United States to the south of us has the highest standard of living in the world and the highest wage structure. Wages in the industrial sector are such that our industrial workers crave parity with their counterparts in the United States. Let us compare what we have done for our dairy farmers in marketing milk with what has been done in the richest nation of the world.
As of April 1 this year when our policy became a $4 policy f.o.b. the factory, the United States policy-I am not criticizing them in any way because they are doing a wonderful job-was $3.50. Singularly important is the fact that just four days ago, three months after this government gave leadership in this regard, the United States amended its policy and pushed up their support level. They make no direct payments such as we do here, in order to keep the cost to the consumer down. The United States increased its support level so that in respect of 3.73 per cent milk, which is a higher percentage than ours, the level will be $4. With 3.5 milk the level would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3.75, or 25 cents lower than ours.
I am not saying for a moment that the needs of the farmers are not great or that we here in this house and this government need not do all that we possibly can to improve their lot. I have said on many occasions that I would be the first to agree that farmers of this country have not kept up on a commensurate basis with improved income conditions in this country, or with the lot of their industrial counterpart. Again the record should be set straight and I am sure the farmers would want it that way.
Let us see what the income of the farmer was when hon. gentlemen opposite were in government and let us see what has happened to it since. I refer to statistics contained in a pamphlet entitled "General Information on Agriculture in Canada", prepared by the economics branch of the Canada
Interim Supply
Department of Agriculture. It is dated October, 1965.
The total income of farmers in millions in 1959 was $2,791. It went down to $2,777 in 1960. That was not a very good year. It went up from $2,777 to $2,952 in 1961, an increase of roughly $180. In 1962 it went up to $3,116; in 1963 to $3,185 and in 1964 it went up to $3,456. Let me point out that during the period of time following our assumption of office the farmers' income position improved by 23 per cent.
Let us take a look at the cost of farm operations during the same period of time. According to the statistics I have in this same pamphlet farm costs during the same period increased by 22 per cent. Hon. members are 100 per cent correct, and I quite agree, that during the same period the industrial worker did not just hold his own as did the farmer; he surged ahead. This is the kind of thing we must do for the farm community as well.
I want to make sure that the complete story is told in an accurate way, and I know that hon. members, just as do the farmers, want the same thing. There has been some difficulty with respect to manufactured milk even since our policy was announced. I am not suggesting that we have achieved a millennium. I hope to do much more for our dairy farmers if I am able, have the ability and can see how to do that. Every farm organization in the country supported our policy which was based on the recommendations of the Federation of Agriculture and the Farmers Union of Canada. They approved this policy and I still believe that it is no worse two months later than April of this year.
What has happened in the interim to create the difficulties which have exercised hon. gentlemen opposite? The province of Ontario fixed a price, quite properly, as we anticipated it would. I commend the minister of agriculture of that great province for so doing. The province of Quebec has special conditions in respect of the production of casein, which is a submarginal product. Unfortunately that province, rightly or wrongly, felt it could not fix the price.
The province of Quebec decided to pay a special subsidy, as an hon. gentleman has said. I did not intend to discuss this matter until the hon. gentleman did so, because I think that is the source of many of the problems with which that hon. minister is faced. In any event, the payment of this extra subsidy in that province has influenced the

July 7, 1966
Interim Supply
Ontario dairy farmers to suggest that if Quebec can pay an extra subsidy of 17J cents in the summer and 35 cents in the winter, the rich province of Ontario ought to be able to do likewise. I do not intend to minimize the problems of the minister of agriculture of Ontario, but this is one problem he has encountered. I should like to see the day come when stabilization programs are completely federal, because I think they would work best that way. In any event, the province of Quebec decided in its wisdom to pay these subsidies and Ontario farmers are now asking for the same.
Some Ontario manufacturers increased the cost of transportation to the farmers and cut off the subsidies on farm storage tanks. The Milk Marketing Board of Ontario has now enacted a regulation to prevent added transportation costs from being tacked on the farmers' costs. Surely this is a clear admission that this is the responsibility of the province. They have now quite properly assumed that responsibility. With those facts being as they are, it would be completely incorrect to imply that these added costs of transportation were in any way within the control of the federal government.
I saw statistics today in respect of the province of Quebec which indicate that not everyone is receiving $4 per 100 pounds. There are marginal areas where there is no competition or market for milk, and because the province of Quebec has not seen fit to fix the price the producers in those areas are receiving less. On the other hand, these statistics show that 80 per cent of milk produced in the province of Quebec is being sold by the farmer for $3.25 or more. They are receiving in addition 75 cents per 100 from the federal treasury and 17J cents from the province of Quebec.
Eighty per cent of the milk is getting $4.17 or more from the province of Quebec.
Hear, hear.

May I ask the minister a question?
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)

I should like to finish my statement, first, if I may, and then I will answer all the questions you like.
I do not wish to minimize the difficulties with which the minister of agriculture in the province of Ontario is faced. I say, with all candour and irrespective of political persuasion, that I found him to be an extremely capable gentleman and a fine minister of

agriculture. I have tried to work with him, and I am sure he has tried to work with me in the best interest of the farming community. It is an unfortunate set of circumstances that the provincial subsidy paid in the province of Quebec has made life politically difficult for him. As I say, I did not intend to raise this matter or to add in any way to his problems until the hon. member for Kent, Ont., raised it in the house tonight, and I therefore felt bound to defend our position.
I do think that this problem between Ontario, Quebec and the federal government has to be worked out. I do not think they contribute to its solution by trying to shove the blame on to the federal government so as to get rid of the difficulty which exists between the two provinces. I realize that that is the name of the game, and that is what they are trying to do. I do not think this will contribute to an ultimate solution which will be in the best interests of the farmer. We have to arrive at some method whereby the stabilization program will be handled at the federal level without provincial subsidies upsetting the applecart. In saying this, I take the very same view as that taken by the Ontario minister in the current year. We may have to find some method of effecting the resolution of this difficult imbalance in Ontario. We have to look into the question of whether the support price enables the factories to pay $3.25, because that is the policy to which we are pledged. If the support price is not sufficient, we will review and revise it whenever necessary to enable the factories to pay that price.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that our policy is the best ever conceived. It is one that is even superior to the policy in the United States of America. It is the greatest increase that the dairy producers have ever received in any one year. I disagree with the allegation that the program has deteriorated in the last two months. It is what the dairy community of Canada wanted, and we have given it to them. I do not think we are doing any service by trying to tear down the federal program because of these teething problems that have arisen between Ontario and Quebec. I think this criticism will in the long run be doing a disservice to the farming community, rather than remedying the difficulties as we should all be trying to do.

Mr. Chairman, they were used at the Quebec conference and I am satisfied they are correct. I do not know whether the hon. member has more authentic statistics. I have listened to some questionable evidence which he quoted earlier this evening, but if he has any more reliable statistics I would be interested to see them. However, if his statistics are no better than his usual fiscal theories they will not be too good either.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister if one must conclude from this that the Quebec minister of agriculture, who was in Ottawa today, showed him statistics indicating that 80 per cent of manufacturing milk in the province of Quebec got a minimum $3.25 per hundredweight, plus 75 cents in the form of a subsidy from the federal government and 17J cents from the provincial government.
Must we conclude, Mr. Chairman, that those figures were given to him by the Quebec minister of agriculture?
Mr. Chairman, I think that our statistics are worth more than the minister's, because ours come from the farmers. As a matter of fact, they tell us: The policy of $4 per hundredweight of milk has never been applied and we are far from getting $4 per hundredweight of milk.
I think that the best statistics are what the farmer is getting. That is what I call statistics. The way they are compiled is probably another matter, but what the farmer is getting is what counts. Here is the concrete, realistic and practical fact of life: how much the farmer is getting for his manufacturing milk. Those are statistics for you.
Mr. Chairman, the minister has given us comparative figures. I would also like to give him the increase in the farmers' production costs.
Since the minister does not want to give us an answer, I would also like to have the opportunity to check if his statistics were given him by the provincial minister of agriculture. He told us: that was given us at a meeting with the provincial minister of agriculture, but he did not tell us if that was given him by the provincial minister of agriculture. That makes all the difference.
Mr. Chairman, we want to check the few facts given by the minister; we want to have the opportunity to pursue that matter and that is why I ask you to call it ten o'clock.
Ten o'clock.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion EXPO '67-INQUIRY AS TO REPRESENTATION OF AGRICULTURE

Mr. Speaker, I bring a matter before the house this evening arising out of my question put to the hon. Minister of Agriculture this afternoon, in which I asked the minister if he would assure the house that the Canadian agriculture industry will have suitable and prominent representation in the form of displays and exhibits at Expo '67, which will be Canada's great centennial exhibition next year at Montreal. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, knowing the minister, that the answer to this question, as I hope, will be in the affirmative.
My question also arises as a result of the recent visit which some of us of this chamber, and members of the other place, made to the site of Expo. We were all very much impressed by the progress being made on this unique project, and I know that every Canadian wishes nothing but success for this great world's fair, this world in 1,000 acres, rising on the bosom of the St. Lawrence river, with our great Canadian metropolis, Montreal, as a backdrop, and truly the urban sponsor of this fair.
We know now that from April 28 to October 27, 1967, more than 70 nations will be exhibiting here in Canada their traditions and cultures, their industrial development, and their products, and of course all their hopes for the future.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Canada, in turn, will be showing her best to the world. Since in any brochures we have received I have not noticed any prominent mention of our third oldest primary industry, agriculture, that is why I have asked my question. As a result of this I would hope that this industry would have prominence at this fair.
I know all hon. members will agree that we must not only maintain, but that we must annually increase our export trade in agricultural products. I was particularly impressed this afternoon by the remarks made by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) when he spoke on the banking resolution and stressed the imperative value of export trade. Exhibits covering all our agronomy with each province represented under the suzerainty of the federal Department of Agriculture will be a most effective factor in promoting and increasing our export trade.
July 7. 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Hon. members will agree that our oldest industry is probably fisheries, dating from the days of John Cabot. Our second oldest industry is the fur trade, dating from the days of Cartier and Champlain; and then the third in age, but most important of all, is agriculture, dating from the life of Louis Hebert, Canada's first farmer who tilled the rough and unwilling soil outside Quebec city in 1620.
The theme that has been accepted for this exhibition "Man and His World" is indeed an inspiration leading down through many lanes of endeavour-Man the Creator, Man the Explorer, Man the Producer, Man and the Community, and Man the Provider. Each of these themes is an attribute to agriculture. In these times when we are becoming, in a sense, more self-assertive and more confident in our accomplishments in our provinces and in our various communities and regions across this great country, this theme and its five sub-themes should certainly be the factor which will unite all Canada and all Canadians and all communities and all Canada's provinces heart and soul into one federal whole, as we play host to the world in our centennial year.
This is why I say that agriculture, now our most important primary industry, must have proper prominence at this exposition. Canada, barely one hundred years old and with a population of not quite twenty million is already, and has for a long time been, a "have" nation. For this heavenly blessing alone we should be very thankful. Think of the many nations of the world who are the "have-nots."
Here is our opportunity-the opportunity for Canadian agriculture to serve our fellowmen the world over, and to feed the hungry. Here is an opportunity for Canadian agriculture to feed our own people better because, in spite of our abundance, there are many people in Canada who can benefit from more food.
I represent the riding of Prince Edward-Lennox, famous for the products of the soil, the farm, the orchard and the dairy industry, and I know my people are always mindful of the importance of advertising and making known the value and high quality of their many and varied commodities.
We know that because of automation and more efficient farm machinery, one man can now produce as much as four did 50 years ago. But we are also concerned because of the fact that many of our broad Canadian acres
that used to produce food lie dormant and forgotten, their former agricultural masters now only a memory.
The responsibilities and the inspiration of Expo should be enough to urge Canadians and the Canadian agricultural industry into a rejuvenation, into reorganization of this industry to break new ground, and take our rightful place as the feeders of millions of hungry mouths in the world. That is why I urge the minister and the Department of Agriculture to bend all their efforts to this task.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. member that the time allotted to him has expired.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bruce S. Beer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I speak for the minister, and I am sure for the whole house, in expressing our appreciation to the hon. member for his very eloquent address on this most interesting and agreeable subject. We are all tremendously interested in Canada's 100th birthday, which we plan for in 1967. Associated with it, of course, will be Expo '67 when Canada will be putting her best foot forward, and displaying herself in this show window of Canada, for the world to see.
As the hon. member has said, agriculture is the third oldest industry in this country. It is fair to say that agriculture primarily developed this country, and certainly the group who played such an important part in developing Canada are not going to be missing when we celebrate our 100th birthday.
At Expo there will be a special agriculture pavilion in which the great wealth of our agricultural products will be displayed. Not only will the primary producers in agriculture be present, but a lot of corporate citizens who are associated with the agriculture industry and perform a great service to this country in the food business, the machinery industry, or in the dairy products industry will also be represented and pulling their full share of the load.
I am not exactly sure what the hon. member's question was, but I have pleasure in assuring him that Canadian agriculture will be represented and that we will be putting our best foot forward.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.30 p.m.

Friday, July 8, 1966.
